Eureka! That makes sense.

The config.yaml in the package is slightly different than the "default", 
and those difference affect how the iotedged works.

1) Try this:

```
sudo apt-get remove iotedge
sudo rm /etc/iotedge/config.yaml
sudo apt-get install <iotedged package>
```

When you edit /etc/iotedge/config.yaml, only replace the `<ADD DEVICE CONNECTION STRING HERE>` with your connection string. 
`sudo systemctl restart iotedge`

That should get you going without any trouble.

2) You aren't the only person having this problem, so I'm going to suggest a revision to our documentation to make this more clear.

Thank you!

[2018-07-24T19:38:07Z | RobertLucian | comment]
The bug seems to be caused by the HW bug with the I2C interface on the Raspberry Pi, where the clock stretching functionality doesn't seem to work well. Apparently, the Pi recognizes a clock stretch if the signal line is kept low and when it rises again it doesn't take into consideration the clock stretch that happened and thus the positive pulse gets to be too narrow (say less than the regular 7.6 uS).

Here's how it looks like when the stretching is done badly:

![analyser](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/26958764/43161475-e8a1bb6e-8f90-11e8-8e95-60d0f08d1f64.PNG)

More can be read here: https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux/issues/254

Anyway, lowering or speeding up the I2C rate is rather cumbersome (and prone to changes with each new release) on the Pi and that's something that we shouldn't do.
Using software serial on the Pi could be a good idea but again, we would need a library that's solid and well tested by the community. 
Using delays in the firmware would have been a good idea, but the default implementation hides away the actual process when the data is sent back to the master. Currently the data is loaded in an ISR-triggerred function by using `Wire.write` s which actually don't send anything until the function ends - this basically takes away the ability to add delays when doing the actual transmission.

My best bet was to identify each transmission by an ID and thus not accept any transfer that comes in. So far it works, but it's not the perfect solution because it doesn't fully solve it - bad values still get through but at a lower rate, which I'd say it's a success.

The best thing we could do is use SPI instead, but unfortunately we are bound by our hardware.

@fengjing1009 As you created the issue with Chinese, I would restate the problem you mentioned for others to know the context.

**Problem:** 
Not able to run multiple nginx pods (with exactly the same nginx image) on the same edge node. 

**How to reproduce it:** 
The problem was tested with the 3 yaml files you provided above (test.yaml, test1.yaml, test2.yaml). First creating a deployment with test.yaml and it works fine. Then creating deployment with test1.yaml or test2.yaml, the container cannot be created on edge node successfully. 

**Reason:**
The containers running on edge node use Host network. This means:
1. The containerPort and hostPort specified in the deployment should be the same. This is why test1.yaml cannot work. Please refer to https://github.com/kubeedge/kubeedge/blob/master/docs/getting-started/usage.md "Deploy Application" section.
2. The same edge node cannot run two containers listening on the same port, this will cause port conflict problem. This is why test2.yaml cannot work. It specifies the ports as 8080, but actually the nginx configuration in nginx:1.15.12 image specifies the port as 80. So, the container still starts with port 80 but this port was already used by the container started with test.yaml.

**How to run 2 nginx pods on the same edge node?**
It requires these two pods listening on different ports. I created a new nginx image **shouhong/nginx-81:1.15.12** with configuration listen on port 81. You can update test1.yaml/test2.yaml with this image name and update the containerPort and hostPort to 81 to have a try. It should work well together with test.yaml.

[2016-12-02T17:50:04Z | aribeironovaes | comment]
Hi @barnstee, 

Thanks for raising this. So, here is what we came: 
So, I tested and you are right, for a .NET module develop the latest change we make can cause a regression. 

Although we think that the current implementation is better than the previous one for the following reason:
Before the configuration just accepted pure String Configuration (like the one you are using on OPC US MODULE “devicekey;somethingelse”. Now the user can actually put JSON value (include pure strings). 

So, just to summarize: 

Before we used to have: 
            "args": {
                "dotnet_module_args": "module configuration"
            }

And the DotNEt Module received: module configuration as it’s content.

Now we are proposing having things like this: 
            "args": "module configuration"
Or 
            "args": {
                    "arg1": "value1",
                    "arg2": "value2"
                    }

And you would receive on your DotNEt Module: 
\”module configuration\”
Or
{\"arg1\":\"value1\",\"arg2\":\"value2\"}


And we now can claim that we support all types of JSON (Which we couldn’t do before). 
Example this: 
[
                {
                    "firstName": "John",
                    "lastName": "Doe"
                },
                {
                    "firstName": "Anna",
                    "lastName": "Smith"
                },
                {
                    "firstName": "Peter",
                    "lastName": "Jones"
                }
            ]
Would turn into this on our .NET Module
[{\"firstName\":\"John\",\"lastName\":\"Doe\"},{\"firstName\":\"Anna\",\"lastName\":\"Smith\"},{\"firstName\":\"Peter\",\"lastName\":\"Jones\"}]

This one the only thing you should do on your module would be to parse whatever you receive as JSON. 


So, with that, I will go ahead and close the issue. 

Thanks a lot Erich!

Angelo Ribeiro.

What we want to be happening, is that the `gpio.ServoDriver` should be passing along the angle value to `adaptor.ServoWrite()`. Then the specific adaptor can handle it however it needs to. So the conversion logic should be in the adaptor, not the `ServoDriver`.

Correct after hard reset, all associations the controller had are lost. 

I'll try go give a better example 

network a: 

 	* node 1 - controller (label = controller)
 	* node 2 - switch (label = lamp)
 	* node 3 - repeater ( label = )
 	* node 4 - sensor (label = door )

<trigger a hard reset> 

network b: (new network after reset, label are still read from
nodes.json) 

 	* node 1- controller (label = controller)

If we then include the repeater again: 

 	* node 1 - controller (label = controller)
 	* node 2 - reapter (label = lamp)

Node 2 now has the label from the network as it was before the hard
reset. This is most cerntainly not what most people woul expect. 

I think there are 2 ways to solve this 

1. delete node.json on a hard reset (easy)
2. include the network id in the filename for the labels so the file is
called nodes_0xXXXXXXXX.json 

And the correct nodes.json is loaded depending on the current network. 
But the later is more complex and probably not worth it.

This definitely is a pain. The root-cause for all this is the fact that we actually are running more or less a complete runtime framework inside the designer. To my understanding we are doing this mainly to allow the scripts and rules (i.e. Xbase) to use the classpath for looking up what kind of commands should be there. IMHO this completely sucks.

For sure, Xbase _by default_ uses the classpath to resolve its stuff. However, this does not have to stay like that. This would "break" the concept that the designer is a real standalone one, because without the connection to the runtime it cannot tell which extensions are there. But let's face it: It is broken today too.

[2016-12-30T17:27:51Z | m-mcgowan | review_comment]
The problem isn't null terminating the local buffer, but that it's copying too much data into the buffer.  We can't null terminate the `cstr` at the given length since that's input data (and const).

[2016-12-30T17:30:29Z | m-mcgowan | review_comment]
Oh, I see what you mean, Using a char instead of an int. Sure we can do that.

[2016-12-30T17:32:23Z | m-mcgowan | comment]
I was unsure how to test it when I found the bug (how to test corrupt heap?) but on reflection it's simple. 

If we can pre-size the internal buffer to be larger than the input string (say 10 chars) and then provide a string that is 7 chars long, with a length of 5, then we verify that only 5 chars were copied to the buffer, and not 7.  (And with the buffer being larger, there is no memory corruption so we don't corrupt the test runner.)

I'll add this test when I'm back from vacation (if someone doesn't beat me to it.)

[2016-11-22T17:52:49Z | flaviostutz | comment]
Marvin,

For that kind of retry, a common practice is to retry in doubles of time from the last time to avoid flooding when an error won't be fixed in a long time. 
For example:
- first try: 1s
- second try: 2s
- 4s, 8s, 16s... 1h, 2h... 6h, 12h...

Many implementations also limits max delay time to avoid getting month delayed retries...

Just a tip...

Flávio Stutz

n = retry count, up to 6 (2^6 = 64)

[2017-01-18T13:57:19Z | yphuangms | comment]
In **iothubtransport_mqtt_command.c**

In IoTHubTransport_MQTT_Common_DoWork() calls to InitializeConnection().

In InitializeConnection(), if (!transport_data->isConnected) then calls to SendMqttConnectMsg().

In SendMqttConnectMsg() calls to mqtt_client_connect()

In mqtt_client_connect(), if fail to connect, NO IotHubClient_LL_ConnectionStatusCallBack will be called if connection failed.

The above call stack shows why a connection failure will never be reported if  "transport_data->isConnected == false". This is the factor that result in different behavior to the call to "IoTHubClient_LL_SendEventAsync()".

### Behavior 1:
If "SendEvent" is executed at the condition of "transport_data->isConnected == true", EventConfirmation callback will be called with an error report, and the **D2C message will be aborted and dropped**. In fact, all the messages in the queue will be aborted for they are processed within one DoWork() call. 

**The consecutive SendEvent calls will be executed in the next DoWork() cycle, the EventConfirmation callback behavior will become "Behavior 2".**

### Behavior 2:
If "SendEvent" is executed at the condition of "transport_data->isConnected == false", EventConfirmation  will never be invoked, a underlying connection retry will be run **until network resumed and connection being recovered the message will be sent to IoTHub, a EventConfirmation callback will be called with a "OK" report**.

[2017-01-20T00:45:01Z | BertKleewein | comment]
Regarding the connection status callback, I have a fix in  progress.  

Regarding the second issue: 
> So the message sent callback might have two different result in corresponding to network disconnection, one is callback with error, the other is no callback or a callback with timeout error.

It appears that we have a timing issue here.  Our SDK will queue messages if the network is not available.  We have a retry policy in place which will try to reconnect to the service with an exponential backoff.  If the SDK is not able to connect. it will retain the message in its queue until a connection can acquired or the timeout period expires.

The timing issue is that a network disconnection that happens in the middle of sending a message will cause a failure to be returned to the client.

In this way, you get an inconsistent behavior depending on the timing of the disconnect.  Most of the time, lack of a network connection will cause the message to be queued.  If you happen to hit a disconnect window, where the disconnection event takes place while the SDK is in the middle of sending a message, then that message will be aborted.  This is by design because the SDK only knows that a network error has taken place while sending the message.  It does not know what caused that error.  Since it's possible that the contents of the message caused the network error, it is better to return failure to the caller rather than re-queue the (possibly harmful) message and risk another network errror.

If you would like to introduce consistency by causing your messages to "fail quickly" when the network is not available, you should be able to set a short timeout as follows:
```
            tickcounter_ms_t timeout = 5000;
            IoTHubClient_LL_SetOption(iotHubClientHandle, "messageTimeout", &timeout);
```

Regarding the second problem, I hope I was able to provide sufficient explanation and maybe some workarounds.  It's also possible the fix for the first issue will help handle the second issue (though I was unable to prove this to myself).

I will respond again to this issue when I have the fix checked into the repo.  I will close the issue when the fix is released.

[2019-08-10T16:49:46Z | anyushun | comment]
How to resolve it?
### Precondition
1. EdgeController create CRD NodeService(means **Node** that needs access to the **Service**)
```
type NodeServiceSpec struct {
    Node   string
    Service string
}
```

### Query service and pods behind it
1. EdgeMesh query service and pods behind it from edgecontroller when client pod access a domain name like ```{name}.{namespace}.svc.{cluster}```
2. EdgeController create NodeService when receive query service or pods behind service
3. Response to EdgeMesh
    1. Service and pods behind it when found, meatamanager save it
    2. NotFound type message when not found, metamanager do not save it

**_note: In order to prevent malicious attacks, traffic control needs to be considered in the product version._**

### Sync service and pods behind it
1. EdgeController watch NodeService and cache as 
```
sync.Map{
    "service.namespace/service.name": []string{"node.name"},
}
```
2. Controller watch service and endpoint. Get all nodes from cache and then sync service and pods behind it to these nodes

[2019-01-21T09:51:14Z | calohmn | review_comment]
Looking at the [spec](http://docs.oasis-open.org/amqp/core/v1.0/os/amqp-core-messaging-v1.0-os.html#type-modified) and for example this [qpid ticket](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/DISPATCH-366), I think we should look at the values of the _modified_ fields here:
````
delivery-failed	        count the transfer as an unsuccessful delivery attempt
undeliverable-here	prevent redelivery
````
So, if `undeliverable-here` is `true`, I think we should probably send back 400 `HTTP_BAD_REQUEST` (same as in `rejected` case). 
If `delivery-failed` is `true`, it looks to me as if we probably should return a status so that the client tries again - which would point to 503 `HTTP_UNAVAILABLE`. WDYT`?

[2016-06-16T11:25:25Z | afuechsel | comment]
I analyzed this a bit. `updateProperties()` actually updates the properties at least in the hue binding, but code is called more than once and the update is only beeing done because of the special implementation in the hue binding. Explanation: 

E.g. the hue binding sets 3 properties in its `HueLightHandler#initialize()` method: 

```
updateProperty(Thing.PROPERTY_MODEL_ID, modelId);
updateProperty(Thing.PROPERTY_FIRMWARE_VERSION, fullLight.getSoftwareVersion());
//...
updateProperty(Thing.PROPERTY_VENDOR, vendor);
```

What happens, is this: 
1. updateProperty calls `AbstractManagedProvider#update()` that logs a warning "Could not update element with key {} in {}, because it does not exists."
2. `ThingManager#thingUpdated()` is called. It throws an IllegalStateException. 
3. the initialize-Method of the HueLighthandler is left immediately due to this exception
4. This Exception is ccaught in the HueBridgehandler's polling loop
5. Now _only because this is a polling loop_ the initialize() method of the HueLightHandler is called _again_ trying to set the properties _again_ 
6. the first call updateProperty now woul _not_ again throw an exception, due to the check in BasicThingHandler, whether the value has already been set (which has been in the previous call) 
7. the second updateProperty will now be executed, logging again a warning, throwing again an exception and bailing out
8. pollingLoop continues...

Eventually, after several calls of the same code, all properties would be set, several exceptions would have been thrown, several log messages would have been shown... Not an ideal case. 

Bindings without such a loop would bail out at the first exception and no property would be set. 

### Suggestion
- Remove the IllegalStateException being thrown for read-only properties, replacing it with a debug logging
- change the warning logging to a debug as well

I think this is not a bug, it is architectural problem. The Rule class does not have a setUID() method. The uid can be set through the constructor only. In the RuleEngine the addRule() returns a new added rule object (which has uid property), but its caller the RuleRegistry.add(Rule) which is inherited from Registry interface does not return added object.
May be Rule.setUID() method has to be added? 
The other way the uid can be updated through reflection, but I don't like to use reflection.

yes, fixing the return type of the Registry.add() method will be the best solution, but all implementations  of the Registry interface will need to be fixed then

[2016-02-16T13:52:39Z | danchom | comment]

[2016-02-16T14:05:17Z | adimova | comment]

[2016-02-16T14:15:41Z | kaikreuzer | comment]
From http://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc2616.txt:

```
   The Location response-header field is used to redirect the recipient
   to a location other than the Request-URI for completion of the
   request or identification of a new resource. For 201 (Created)
   responses, the Location is that of the new resource which was created
   by the request.
```

So we should imho definitely fill the location header field.
The body of the response can imho remain empty. Alternatively, I would vote for returning the full rule entity back.

> which will be the return type of add(), key or element?

The element as we do not even know what the key is within the AbstractRegistry.

[2017-03-09T09:09:53Z | laurentderu | comment]
The problem is that, for unknown reason, the neighbor entry for your node has been removed from the neighbor table of 6LBR, this is the (null) in the routing table. Because of that, the BR is no longer able to forward the packets towards your node as the next hop of the configured route does not exist anymore.

Now the root cause is not clear to me at all, and as you said, the 6lbr.log file does not show anything useful. To be able to analyse further, you should enable the traces in uip-ds6-nbr and maybe also in uip-ds6-route, rpl-dag and rpl-icmp6.
Note that 6LBR 1.4.x is still based on Contiki 3.0, on the other hand, 6LBR 1.5.x, the current develop branch, is based on the latest version of Contiki which contains updates and fixes related to the neighbor table management. It quite possible that you are observing a bug that is already solved, so before digging too much into the issue I would suggest to try with the latest version of the develop branch.

Btw, the ping you observe is in fact not related to RPL, it's a feature of the cc26xx-web-demo firmware which ping periodically its parent to get the current RSSI.

[2017-03-15T09:09:55Z | laurentderu | comment]
In a RPL network, a downward route is only created when a valid DAO message is received. If a data packet is received from a node, a route is not created, otherwise you could have several downward routes towards the same node, some of them even not working as the radio conditions have changed.

In Contiki, the route created by RPL are protected, meaning that a route (and the corresponding next hop) will only be removed when an explicit No Path DAO (remove route message) or if the route lifetime has expired, or if there is a global or local repair.

In your case, the next hop has been deleted without removing the route, so it's most certainly a bug in the Contiki stack.

If you remove a route via the web interface, the end node does not know its route has been deleted so no new route will be created until the previous route lifetime is expired. To force recreation of the route you must trigger a global repair on the RPL page.

It appears that we have found the issue and issued a fix on v1.4.2.

For those who are curious this was caused by bad system time in OctoPi. The clock was going back in some restarts tricking the plugin into thinking that an expired token was still valid. This caused unauthorized errors when using the token which resulted in the user being logged out.

The new version refreshes the token on every new boot thus setting the baseline time to whatever it is at the time of boot.

It appears that the system clock is unreliable in OctoPi. 

I'm going to close the issue now. We can re-open if people with 1.4.2 still see this.

However, when the `ThingManager` then turns to the thing handler, it only checks whether they are initialized:

https://github.com/eclipse/smarthome/blob/5b746e3084ca2803400549bd5467a11c7116d92b/bundles/core/org.eclipse.smarthome.core.thing/src/main/java/org/eclipse/smarthome/core/thing/internal/ThingManager.java#L520-L526

It doesn't care whether the bridge is online or not. The question now is whether it would help if the `ThingManager` would call the child thing handler's `initialize()` _only_ once the bridge becomes ONLINE. Under the assumption that the bridge is required in order to successfully communicate with the device, I think this would make sense. 

Nevertheless, the child handle must be able to cope with the situation that the communication breaks down at any time anyways.

So, TL;DR: No, I don't think this is good to implement this logic in the binding. It puts the same burden on all bindings. This is something which the framework should take care of. IMHO this is a bug.

[2017-07-26T07:46:04Z | sjsf | comment]
Aaaaah, haha, found it... 

In java (and xbase accordingly), a line break has no meaning. And `return` optionally _can_ have an argument. As you left out the semicolons, the interpreter reads it differently from what we humans intuitively would do. It uses the second log stamement as a return value, therefore executing it. When reformatting your code like following, the problem get more clear I think:

```
    logInfo("Info","Änderung SV Temperatur erkannt1")
    return logInfo("Info","Änderung SV Temperatur erkannt2")                                                                                                                                                              
``` 

Therefore in this case you need to help the interpreter, eliminating the ambiguity with a semicolon:

```
    logInfo("Info","Änderung SV Temperatur erkannt1")
    return;
    logInfo("Info","Änderung SV Temperatur erkannt2")                                                                                                                                                              
```

I will consider this caveat in my outstanding PR for the documentation.

[2017-07-26T15:50:58Z | sjsf | comment]
Sure, no problem. However, this is not a question of only suppressing a warning - it's none of those warnings that _we_ invented ourselves (that would have been easy then...), but it actually comes from the base language. We of course _could_ change the DSL language definition so that it expects a return value. But then suddenly it's not optional anymore and you would _have_ to return something on _every_ rule. Which would be the much bigger pain.

[2018-12-05T22:06:19Z | jlovinger-particle | comment]
Whatever you guys decide on I'm sure will be OK and all will be equally functional. Improvement on the status quo.

We're kind of getting into the weeds because system_notify_event with this Pull request hides three kinds of behaviors.

Defer initial execution into System thread if running from an interrupt.
Defer final execution into Application thread if running from the System Thread.
Execute immediately if running from the Application Thread (but not an ISR!).

Without really ripping it apart or refactoring it will be hard to make explicitly clear the execution paths without also parsing through the code. For example...

1. ISR interrupts Application Thread and triggers an event
2. Defer event into the System Thread
3. Drop back into the Application Thread
4. Preempt/etc into the System Thread
5. Begin processing event in the System Thread
6. Defer event into the Application Thread
7. Preempt/etc into the Application Thread
8. Process event

None of which is made clear by the old/new names of system_notify_event/system_notify_event_isr OR the new/new with system_notify_event/system_notify_impl.

And on top of that, previously it would have just been...

1. ISR interrupts Application Thread and triggers an event
2. Process event immediately since detects Application Thread context.

Which was likely bad in its own way as the ISR would have been executing like it *was* the Application Thread introducing all sorts of concurrency issues I wonder if people were handling. But if they were it sure would have been responsive...

Unexpected complexity, for sure.

[2016-04-16T14:57:11Z | DavidStacer | comment]
I had this problem too on a Wemos D1-mini. Updating the driver did not solve it.

To diagnose this and see all the message, I connected up another USB serial port adapter. Then connected the RX from the second serial board to the D1-mini TX pin and tied GND to the serial board. I then used Termite terminal program to monitor the serial traffic.

I changed the default Homie baud rate to 74880 - that is ESP8266 default boot baud rate. This allowed me to see the ESP8266 boot up messages too.

Now I could see all of the messages.  When I pulled the main D1-mini USB cable and plugged back in, the majority of the time I would see:
â€¢ SSL: no
  â€¢ OTA
    â€¢ Enabled: no
Flagged for reset by pin
Device is in a resettable state
Configuration erased
â†» Rebooting in config mode

My theory:
When pinMode(this->_interface->reset.triggerPin, INPUT_PULLUP); is executed, the onboard D1-mini USB Serial adapter **may** not let the GPIO0 pin go high right a way. If you look on the D1-mini schematic, the RTS is connected to the GPIO0 pin via resister and NPN transistor. I'm speculating that the PC driver needs to give it a command to change (high or low don't know which).

Placing a delay(50); after the Homie.setup() and before the Homie.loop(); seemed to solve the problem too but I didn't like that as a solution.

Looking much deeper into the bounce code for the switch I found the default state is set to 0 meaning the switch is closed - requesting configuration mode.  In Bounce::attach I changed it to be state=1; as the default.

I have cycled the D1-mini with the USB cable many times and it seems to have fixed the problem of going into configuration mode without pressing and holding the switch.

Changing that line did fix it for me because [Bounce attach()](https://github.com/thomasfredericks/Bounce2/blob/master/Bounce2.cpp#L25) sets the default to 0 but 1 would be a better default for this application.

When _handleReset call is made to [_resetDebuncer.read()](https://github.com/marvinroger/homie-esp8266/blob/master/src/Homie/Boot/BootNormal.cpp#L292l) it just returns the current  [Bounce::read()](https://github.com/thomasfredericks/Bounce2/blob/master/Bounce2.cpp#L87) value. The current state is still low because [update()](https://github.com/marvinroger/homie-esp8266/blob/master/src/Homie/Boot/BootNormal.cpp#L290) has only been called one time, so we really are not getting a debounced reading but just the initial reading.

I think its hard to fix in Homie but maybe don't call the _resetDebuncer.read() until the [DEFAULT_RESET_TIME](https://github.com/marvinroger/homie-esp8266/blob/master/src/Homie/Constants.hpp#L18) has passed since boot up but that is just another way of delaying. I was having a similar problem and came across this issue.  The solution wasn't immediately clear, so I'm summarizing to help others who also get here and are confused:

If your WeMos D1 Mini loses its configuration when you plug it into your computer with USB, it is probably erroneously detecting the RTS/DTS wiring in the WeMos as a request to reset and delete the configuration.

You can disable the reset trigger completely with Homie.disableResetTrigger() and it will stop deleting the config.  If you want the reset trigger behavior, you may be able to move it to another pin.  I have not attempted this.

[2019-09-30T14:10:09Z | calohmn | comment]
@selobosi Looking at the log file, the `cannot create concurrent command consumer` error comes *before* the AMQP adapter takes notice of the connection not being active anymore (`lost connection to device`). The period between the `STOPPING NETWORK` mark and the time that the adapter notices that is more than a minute. 
Have you tried setting the idle timeout when opening the connection to the AMQP adapter to a value lower than that?

The idleTimeout check that the AMQP adapter is doing on the connection takes both the idleTimeout advertised by the client as well as the local idleTimeout of the AMQP server (currently not set) into account. I think we should make the idleTimeout / heartbeat of the AMQP server of the AMQP adapter configurable to better handle situations like the above. 
Until then, you could try setting the idle timeout in your client.
As long as the idleTimeout check notices the inactive connection _before_ the device opens a new command consumer, just from looking at the code and the log output above, I think the above error shouldn't occur.

[2019-10-15T06:47:15Z | sophokles73 | comment]
Ok, as it turns out, the AMQP adapter does not set an idle-time-out at all in its open frame, i.e. the AMQP adapter does not ask its peers (the devices) to prevent a timeout at all.
Given that the vertx-proton library only allows to set the (server side) idle-time-out value as part of binding the server to a port, we cannot use tenant specific values here but instead need to set a value at the adapter level.

@selobosi The idle time out handling is done in the [vertx-proton library](https://github.com/vert-x3/vertx-proton/blob/679fd2e2ca1d0d16eadd53a6fc2754c4c0056090/src/main/java/io/vertx/proton/impl/ProtonTransport.java#L220). However, I think that the explanation given in the AMQP 1.0 spec will be more helpful for understanding how this is supposed to work.

The way the AMQP adapter is currently implemented, it has little chance of detecting that the network connection to a device has broken down, so I consider this a bug.
Devices should also include an idle-time-out in their open frame in order to make the AMQP adapter send empty frames periodically if no commands are due for the device. That way the device can try to gracefully close the connection when it times out and then try to re-connect. If the connection was still alive at the time the device sent its close frame and the adapter actually received it, the adapter can then do its house keeping and close the downstream command consumer so that the device's next subscription request should succeed again ...

Hi all, 

this is caused by the fact that CRON does not directly aware of the timezone. To avoid any problem with the server timezone (which is often depending on the underlying OS) I've set all CRON expression created to be based on UTC. 

The solution proposed by Aleksandra remove this forcing to UTC, but if (if I'm correct) make thing work only when the timezone of the browser is matching the timezone of the server, and would definitely not work with users from different timezones. 

i.e.:
User A creates a CRON with his timezone (+2:00 for example) like:
Starts: 10:00
End: 12:00
CRON: `0 0 12 * * ?`

User B views/edits the trigger from another timezone (+5:00 for example) and sees
Starts: 13:00
End: 15:00
CRON: `0 0 12 * * ?` <-- same problem, since CRON does not have any link to the timezone from which is created.

Moreover, if the trigger is created/retrieved/managed from the REST API we will not have any info about the User's timezone from the browser.

Let me know what you think.

As an alternative solution I would try to make clear that CRON is in UTC.

Regards,

_Alberto_

@edubovik @demon-xxi @YermakovSergiy @Pilatuz @Nikolay-Kha @vyrostkov @vktk 

API change request for poll/pollMany.

Implemented by .net server existing protocol

```
pollMany: [ {guid, commandT1}, {guid, commandT1}, ... ]
poll: [{commandT1}, {commandT1}, ...]
```

where commandT1 object does not contain device guid, while option is to change conversation response to 

```
pollMany: [ {commandT2}, {commandT2}, ... ]
poll: [{commandT2}, {commandT2}, ...]
```

where commandT2 object does contain device guid.

Java server provides:

```
pollMany: [ {guid, commandT2}, {guid, commandT2}, ... ]
poll: [{commandT2}, {commandT2}, ...]
```

Feel free to provide your responses.

[2015-12-16T16:17:46Z | demon-xxi | comment]
I think it is important to maintain same contract for the Command entity regardless of the method called (poll or pollMany). That will minimize complexity on the client side too. So including device guid in the command is the way to go and we can skip it in results. That will affect .net compatibility but not a big migration change to do. 
For better compatibility we can also use protocol versioning in .net and/or java as well. Not sure if we havr time to do so now.

But I am open to discuss to follow a different logic for the rules - i.e. only describing the status of a rule itself (and NOT_INITIALIZED simply means that there is some issue with a handler, be it that they are not there or that something is misconfigured). The values which were getting overwritten on other readings was caused by bad timing on the GrovePi and a lack of organizing the requests one after the another in an orderly manner. 

A mechanism to check if there's available data on the GrovePi has been added which basically reduces the need to use `sleep`s on the Pi. Now, we can just poll the GrovePi until it gets a response for the requested data. 

Huge improvements to the sample rate on basic functions (reading/writing on digital/analog ports, ultrasonic sensor, etc) have been brought. Before these improvements, in order to have a reliable connection to the GrovePi and still be able to poll the GrovePi for values (or for writing to ports) a sample rate of 10-15 was doable - now we can see sample rates of up to 380 while the system is running without any hiccups.

The DHT sensor at the moment takes roughly 550 ms for a reading. I think that number can be brought down to a half. It still needs to be investigated.

[2018-07-11T12:03:24Z | RobertLucian | comment]
The firmware would resort to reading twice for both the temperature and humidity sensor (with the DHT11) and that was quite inefficient. I have come up with another function in the firmware that does both of them in one run, thus taking the reading time down to ~280ms (up to 3.54 samples / sec from ~1.7 samples / sec).

[2018-07-11T18:12:28Z | RobertLucian | comment]

[2018-02-20T21:55:36Z | ikalchev | comment]
What follows is a guess, but I am very confident this is exactly what happens:

## Background
When iOS connects to an Accessory, it doesn't close the connection (socket) - it keeps it alive and doesn't say when it leaves (makes sense, because phones move, go to sleep, etc.). It is the accessory's responsibility to "expect" a dead connection.

So using this keep-alive connection, the accessory can send an event, which is what happens when you call `set_value(value, should_notify=True)`. But because the connection could be stale, HAP-python sets a timeout of 3 seconds for the send and if it doesn't happen, it shuts down the connection. After the send the timeout is removed.

On the same connection, iOS can decide to make a HTTP request, such as "set this value to this accessory" and waits for a reply to that request.
## The problem
When I set the timeout to None (i.e. no timeout) instead of 3 seconds, the problem vanishes completely. So I think there is some race condition in which the timeout is not removed properly, which causes a timeout in the thread that makes the request reply. What is more, I think that even if you use the "working" solution of ElectronicLock I posted earlier, there is a chance that it will also timeout.

Thanks for focusing my attention on this - I will try to address this ASAP.

[2020-02-18T18:11:57Z | avtolstoy | review_comment]
Why are we removing all the checks for `TOTAL_PINS`? Especially in HAL, which will break backwards compatibility.

It's entirely possible to pass `PIN_INVALID` as the pin or some other invalid number.

[2020-02-19T05:48:23Z | XuGuohui | review_comment]
I don't how it breaks the backwards compatibility. By moving the check routine from wiring to HAL just gains the time that the wiring API acquiring/releasing the lock. Even if user pass invalid pin number, the HAL can still handle it correctly. So from user's perspective, the result calling the wiring API makes no difference. The root cause of the issue is that the `begin()` APIs are not type safe, so when user calling `SPI.begin(SPI_MODE_MASTER)`, it will call the `SPIClass::begin(uint16_t ss_pin)` instead. To fix it I just assign a default value `SPI_DEFAULT_SS` for the second argument of the `SPIClass::begin(SPI_Mode mode, uint16_t ss_pin)` API, so that it can invoke the corresponding overloaded function. If we don't move the check routine to HAL, the wiring API will return immediately if calling `SPI.begin(SPI_MODE_MASTER)`.

My general goal for this refactoring would be to get the whole architecture as much as possible in sync with what we have for Things as there are indeed many many similarities.
In the context of https://github.com/eclipse/smarthome/issues/4993, we will need an enable/disable mechanism for Things and I suggested there to look at the rule engine as we can also enable/disable rules. But as we are just discussing the right structure here, #4993 also depends on this discussion. On the other hand, we can learn a lot from the experiences from the Thing infrastructure, so let me try to give you an overview of how I see the components relate:

| Things | Automation | Description |
|--------|------------|-------------|
| Thing | Rule | The main entity |
| ThingRegistry | RuleRegistry | The passive registry that aggregates providers and offers CRUD operations |
| ManagedThingProvider | ManagedRuleProvider | A special storage-backed provider that the registry delegates to for all write operations |
| ThingManager | RuleEngine | The service that actively instantiates and assigns handlers to entities and deals with their lifecycle |
| ThingHandler | ModuleHandler | The code that backs an entity (resp. parts of it) |
| ThingHandlerCallback | ModuleHandlerCallback | A callback API that gives handlers access to the framework features that they are generally allowed to use |
| Thing.getStatusInfo() | Rule.getStatusInfo() | A transient status information on the entity, which is read-only and managed by the active service (ThingManager/RuleEngine) only. |
| Thing.isEnabled() | Rule.isEnabled() | A transient enablement information on the entity, which is read-only and managed by the active service (ThingManager/RuleEngine) only. |

If nobody vetos, I would try to refactor the automation component accordingly next week, i.e. mainly introducing the transient status/enable information on the entity itself and thus reducing the need to access the RuleEngine.

| ThingHandler | ModuleHandler | The code that backs an entity (resp. parts of it) |
| ThingManagerImpl | RuleManagerImpl | The (internal) service that actively instantiates and assigns handlers to entities and deals with their lifecycle |
| ThingManager | RuleManager | The service that offers "higher-level" functionality like enablement, status information etc. |
| ThingHandlerCallback | ModuleHandlerCallback | A callback API that gives handlers access to the framework features that they are generally allowed to use. Usually similar to the Manager interface. |

1. a configuration property of the ItemChannelLink
2. the binding's preference for a channel
3. the binding's preference generally
4. and "auto-update = true" as a default if none of the above gave any clue (in order to preserve compatibility).

mariadb in current distros (tested on Ubuntu 16.04) is set with:

collation-server      = utf8mb4_general_ci

I have noticed that the timing in the `grovepi.py` script isn't handled in all places. 

I realized that when I tried to poll the dust sensor faster at higher rates without adding any delay between the I2C calls. When I would do that, the dust sensor function would no longer notify me of new values through the `databack[0]` parameter:
```
def dustSensorRead():
	"""
	By default, the sample rate is set to 1 at every 30 seconds and this
	function was written only for that interval.

	If you wish to use a different
	interval, then use dustSensorReadMore function. To set a
	different interval, use setDustSensrInterval function.
	"""
	write_i2c_block(address, dus_sensor_read_cmd + [unused, unused, unused])
	time.sleep(.2)
	#read_i2c_byte(address)
	#number = read_i2c_block(address)
	#return (number[1] * 256 + number[2])
	data_back= bus.read_i2c_block_data(address, 1)[0:6]
	#print data_back[:4]
	if data_back[0]!=255:
		lowpulseoccupancy=(data_back[3] * 65536 + data_back[2] * 256 + data_back[1])
		#print [data_back[0],lowpulseoccupancy]
		return [data_back[0], lowpulseoccupancy]
	else:
		return [-1,-1]
```

Looking at this code of  the `grovepi.py`, I noticed that there's no `time.sleep` after the second I2C call. After adding one in there the dust sensor started working really well. So the problem is that the for loop in the firmware needs some time to run it and when 2 consecutive I2C calls are made with no delay between them, things will get messed. 

What's interesting is that a bunch of functions don't have the 2nd delay added for the 2nd call, which might mean this is the cause for #412 .

[2018-07-17T15:26:50Z | RobertLucian | comment]
Seems like with the new changes that allow a much faster polling rate, the dust sensor no longer reports the correct values when the polling rate is slightly higher than what it used to be. Since this issue ought not to be fixed by adding delays, I resorted to finding the bug and seeing where it actually gets stuck.

After digging some time into this issue, I came to the conclusion that the problem comes from the variable that holds the low pulse occupancy value, whose value gets changed w/o having to when it's being used in the main loop and in the ISR. The problem doesn't come from not being a volatile variable or anything humanly imaginable, but it comes from the fact it was using `unsigned long` as a data type. It seems like when `unsigned longs`  (volatile) are used in both ISRs and the main loop, the variable change's its value without any sense. 

Changing the data type to a 16 bit one seems to mitigate the issue so most likely this is a compiler issue.

I'll try to formalise here our idea on how to solve this issue. The constraints we see are the following:
- we would like to preserve the existing tag. That is the effective tag used to perform the 3.1.0 release and that should be kept as is.
- we would like to not modify the release branch. Indeed, since the changes are already merged into develop, the branch could be easily removed without loosing commits and preserving the linearity of the contributions.
- we would like to have the exists plugin always enabled and give the capability to disable it by selecting a specific profile. In our opinion, having it enabled only during the release process will highlight possible issues too late in the process.

To meet all those requirements, we started a maintenance branch called `maintenance-3.1` that has, as a first commit, a fix for the exists plugin by providing a profile to allow the user the capability to disable it when building.
We will create a new tag named `KURA_3.1.0_RELEASE_AMENDED`.

In this way, all the history is preserved, the developers can use the new tag to build their own Kura 3.1.0 and the exists plugin will be always enabled to prevent errors with versions.

Hope to hear your thoughts on this.

[2020-01-27T12:29:07Z | hanneshoettinger | comment]
You need to set the master port in controller.yaml to 8080:
[https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/controlling-access/](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/controlling-access/)
Default localhost port for Kubernetes is 8080. 6443 is the secure port.
controller.yaml:
`controller:
    kube:
    ...
    master: "http://127.0.0.1:8080" #Note if master and kubeconfig are both set, master will override any value in kubeconfig.`

As described in [https://github.com/kubeedge/kubeedge/blob/master/docs/getting-started/release_package.md](https://github.com/kubeedge/kubeedge/blob/master/docs/getting-started/release_package.md) do also set:
`vi /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
- --insecure-port=8080
- --insecure-bind-address=0.0.0.0`

Single precision floating point doesn't provide large degree of precision and to retain accuracy in performing precise calculations, wires didn't include `floats`.

[2019-06-26T13:53:28Z | weakfl | comment]
@timbms I was actually looking into #269, but since charts are more or less images, I had similar problems as described here.

A couple of observations:

There's a race condition in `NewImageUITableViewCell.loadImage()`:

```
DispatchQueue.main.async {
    self?.widget?.image = image
}
self?.layoutIfNeeded()
self?.layoutSubviews()
if self?.delegate != nil {
    self?.delegate?.didLoadImageOf(self)
}
```

The delegate function `self?.delegate?.didLoadImageOf(self)` is called before `self?.widget?.image = image` is set. This triggers a second call of `loadImage()` when `reloadRows(at:with:)` gets called.
What's the reason to set the widget image asynchronously anyway?

Using `beginUpdates()`/`endUpdates()` instead of `reloadRows(at:with:)` fixes some layout issues for me. And since the cell data doesn't change, reloading the row isn't necessary.

There are still issues with rotation though. After rotating from portrait to landscape **and back** to portrait the cell height is wrong. I have no idea why though :/
Of course you could just call `reloadData()` after rotation to work around the issue, but I'd be interested to know what is causing it in the first place.

I'll submit a (WIP) PR for #269 shortly, maybe you have an idea what's causing the rotation issue.

[2016-11-01T17:44:34Z | marvinroger | comment]
Got it. The default LED pin is `BUILTIN_LED` (https://github.com/esp8266/Arduino/blob/master/variants/generic/pins_arduino.h). On some board, the LED on pin 1 is also the serial line. So your serial was not working correctly because it conflicted with the LED blinking (when connecting to the Wi-Fi). Calling `Homie.setLedPin(16, false);` changes the LED pin, so Serial works back again. If you say the LED does not work, it probably means your LED pin is not actually on GPIO16. Are you sure the LED is on pin 16?

@onkelandy From what I found out, your problem only exists, if you want to address a function for the item itself (eg..: 'sh...changed_by()') and direct ancestors, but not for referencing other items like 'sh..sister.changed_by()'.

Interpreting the dots in another way if parentheses are present gives a lot of other problems. The solution I found is the following: Inserting a reserved word 'self'. 

To reference the item itself you can use '.self' instead of '.'. So instead of writing 'sh...changed_by()' (which produces unexpected results), you could write 'sh..self.changed_by()'.

Or for referencing a function of the parent item, instead of writing 'sh....changed_by()' (which produces unexpected results), you can write 'sh...self.changed_by()'

[2019-09-03T08:19:15Z | sophokles73 | comment]
> This "terminal error" will stop the client from trying to re-connect, and it seems like it never will re-try again. For as long as process is alive. So effectively, the process would be dead now.

The behavior of the protocol adapters has been implemented this way deliberately in order to prevent useless connection attempts to services with which no connection can be established due to misconfiguration (on either the client or server side).

> It looks to me, as if the correct way to signal the "terminal error", is not through the "readiness" check, but through the "liveness" check instead.

I do not think that there is a right or wrong way here. We need to address two different scenarios here:
1. The service we try to connect to is implemented/configured correctly but is not (yet) ready for operation, i.e. it is in the process of starting up or we have temporarily lost network connection to it. In any case, once we are able to reach the service, a connection will be established.
2. The service is wrongly implemented or there is a configuration mismatch between the adapter and the service. This means that no matter how often we try to connect to the adapter, the connection attempt will always fail unless the configuration/implementation is fixed.

The first case is already covered by the current re-connect behavior. 

> Additionally, I would question the idea of a terminal error altogether. From what I see in our case, it has to do with an invalid service credential. So that problem will go away in a minute.

While the problem might be easy to fix (in most cases), whether it happens or not depends on an operator to become aware of it. I agree that with the current implementation this will be hard to detect as the adapter process seems to be running happily while in fact it doesn't try to (re-)establish a connection anymore.

> I think we should:
    Trigger a liveness failure in case of a terminal error.
    Event for a terminal error, allow to try again.

I am not sure what the second item is supposed to mean. But I would rather simply allow the adapter to try to re-connect in case of a terminal error instead of restarting the whole pod based on a failed liveness check, which is much slower and more costly.

FMPOV the readiness check is still the right way to make sure that
1. operators become aware of a problem with the adapter/service
1. allow the adapter to *auto recover* from the existing problem

The liveness check does not add much value here FMPOV because we would use it basically do the same as the HonoClient already does, i.e. trying to establish the connection once more.

However, the startup of the adapter does not need to depend on the successful establishment of the connections to the services because with the re-try behavior of the HonoClient, we already make sure that the connections get established eventually and the readiness check already signals to Kubernetes when this is the case.

[2019-02-21T01:25:41Z | YoDaMa | comment]
The progress on updating the published Arduino libraries of the code is currently blocked as we fix some core problems with previous versions of the published Arduino SDK Libraries. Since the previous versions did not authenticate the connection by exchanging and validating trusted certs to IoT Hub, we are fixing this in the code before moving forward with releasing another version of the libraries.  

In the meantime, to tinker with the latest version of the SDK using Arduino Libraries, you can manually build the libraries locally. This will not fix the sample, just bump the version of the SDK.

**How to manually build the library locally:**
This is using the same process that generates libraries that do not support trusted certs, which means that your devices could be connecting to any spoofed connection point and not validating that it's the actual IoT Hub. **SO DO NOT USE THIS CODE IN PRODUCTION DEVICES**. Only use the manual process for tinkering (as a community also we are happy have you look into some of the library versioning issues, particularly in ESP8266). 

Steps to manually create local versions of Arduino Libraries:

Clone the PAL Repo (you need recursive because the C SDK is included as a submodule): 
```
git clone --recursive https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-pal-arduino.git 
```

Navigate to the build_all directory:
```
cd build_all
```

Run make_sdk.cmd, specifying the location of the Arduino Library on your machine:
```
.\make_sdk.cmd C:\Users\<username>\Documents\Arduino\libraries
```

This'll populate the Arduino libraries with the 4 AzureIoT Libraries using the latest SDK.

 - esp8266 (by ESP8266 community) - 2.4.2

Libraries:
 - Azureiothub - 1.0.45
 - Azureiotprotocol_mqtt - 1.0.45
 - azureiotutility - 1.0.45

[2017-03-15T12:00:36Z | calohmn | comment]
The reason is the `System.in.read()` inside `waitForInput()` which is waiting for ENTER to be pressed.
As this is blocking, it is executed with `vertx.executeBlocking()` (so that is is run in a Vertx worker thread).

But although a Vertx worker thread is supposed to be doing longer-running tasks outside the Vertx event thread, these tasks should not run forever. To promote this, there is `VertxOptions.maxWorkerExecuteTime` (default 60s), causing warnings after this time has elapsed.

A simple solution to this would be removing the `waitForInput` method and letting the application be stopped by pressing CTRL+C ("Press CTRL+C to stop receiver.").
Cleanup work on shutdown can then be done in a @PreDestroy method.

(I would prefer CTRL+C also because it would allow pressing ENTER to add some blank lines in the terminal to better distinguish subsequent log output.)

Yes - it was binding to my openVPN interface (which the brain isn't on).  When an interface isn't defined, the system 'chooses' one (according to doc) - just happen to choose the wrong one.  I made a patch to two of the files (index.js and mdns.js):

In **index.js** - I replaced the findFirstNeeoBrain with the following:

```
function findFirstNeeoBrain() {
    return new BluePromise((resolve, reject) => {
        const nets = os.networkInterfaces();
        for (const netName in nets) {
            const max = nets[netName].length;
            for (var idx = 0; idx < max; idx++) {
                const netInfo = nets[netName][idx];
                if (netInfo.internal === false && netInfo.family == "IPv4") {
                    mdns.findFirstNeeoBrain(netInfo.address)
                        .then(buildNEEOBrainModel)
                        .then(serverInfo => resolve(serverInfo));
                }
            }
        }
    });
}
```

That will loop through all the non-loopback IP4 interfaces and attempt to find the brain using that interface calling...

The **mdns.js** patch for the interface:

```
function findFirstNeeoBrain(netIf) {
  debug('findFirstNeeoBrain');
  return new BluePromise((resolve, reject) => {

    function serviceUpListener(service) {
      if (!service || !service.txt) {
        debug('invalid entry ignored');
        reject(new Error('INVALID_SERVICE_FOUND'));
      }
      debug('found a NEEO Brain: [%s]', service.name);
      resolve(service);
    }
    var bonjour = require('bonjour')({ interface: netIf });
    const mdnsBrowser = bonjour.findOne({ type: MDNS_NAME }, serviceUpListener);
    mdnsBrowser.start();
  });
}
```

Pretty self explanatory - basically create bonjour with the specified interface.

I don't have two brains (yet) so I can't really test to see if this works when each brain is on a different interface - but it looks like it should.

Note: let me know if you want me to submit an official PR with this fix...

[2018-01-27T07:45:34Z | ikalchev | comment]
I looked into that, here is what I found:

You can set the name characteristic, but this has to happen before you pair with iOS:
```python
# This must happen before pairing:
acc = Accessory.create("MyAcc", pincode=b"203-23-999")
s = loader.get_serv_loader().get("TemperatureSensor")
s.add_opt_characteristic(loader.get_char_loader().get("Name"))
acc.add_service(s)
s.get_characteristic("Name").set_value("Foo", False)
# OK, the service will show as Foo when paired
```

However, changing the name after that doesn't work and this is a bug in HAP-python. This is because iOS doesn't know it has new values to read. The way to notify about this, is to change the [config version](pyhap/accessory.py#L121) of the accessory - something I have not implemented yet.

Fortunately, this is not hard to fix and will do so in a few days. Until then, you can workaround this by doing:
```python
# acc is your Accessory.
# driver is the AccessoryDriver that manages acc (as in main.py)
# Change name
acc.get_service("TemperatureSensor").get_characteristic("Name").set_value("new name", False)
# Bump config version
acc.config_version += 1
# Update mDNS information so that iOS clients know they have to re-fetch acc info.
driver.update_advertisment()
# Persist the new config_version (see issue #11)
driver.persist()
```

Thanks for uncovering this, I will try to make it easier to change such optional chars (i.e. without the workaround). Note that for some optional characteristics, like StatusLowBatter, iOS listens for updates, so the workaround is not needed.

[2018-01-28T09:24:05Z | ikalchev | comment]
Change is in. When you make a configuration change, such as adding a Service or changing a characteristic such as Name, you can call:
```python
accessory.config_changed()
```
This notifies iOS clients they need to refetch the whole accessory again and persists the new state of the accessory. Note that although iOS immediately fetches the new config, it does not update the UI immediately. However, the updates are eventually shown.

3. apply the last command(s) as soon as the light is online and proper values have been retrieved

I believe this is because in case of a send error, we end up to this line:

https://github.com/Azure/azure-c-shared-utility/blob/4461e2b09dd9e854865a53a22da894b1b21235d1/adapters/socketio_berkeley.c#L496

The reason I suspect this would be the right behavior is that I can see, for example, the following in the requirements:

```
devdoc/tlsio_arduino_requirements.md:**SRS_TLSIO_ARDUINO_21_056: [** if the ssl was not able to send any byte in the buffer, the tlsio_arduino_send shall call the on_send_complete with IO_SEND_ERROR, and return _LINE_. **]**

Hope its ok for both of you that I am writing something to the problem,  because some days ago I took a look at that area.
1. CANAL_USB2CAN_DRIVER_MAX_OPEN has to be set greater than 1, because the dll driver limits with that the max. number of usb2can objects.
2. In my eyes the "break" in https://github.com/grodansparadis/vscp_software/blob/master/src/vscp/drivers/level1/usb2can/usb2can/common/dlldrvobj.cpp you mentioned Stefan, is necessary. Because the CDllDrvObj::addDriver method searchs for a empty slot and if a empty slot is found, it will assign the usb2can object to this slot and break out of the loop.

If you really change only the CANAL_USB2CAN_DRIVER_MAX_OPEN to e. g. 10, then clean everything and compile it again, it should run.

Your log shows "Failed to open driver. Will not use it!", which is thrown only in case that the handle is lower or equal than 0, not 1681! So it is strange that you see always 1681?! But it would match in case the CANAL_USB2CAN_DRIVER_MAX_OPEN is set to 1.

Please add a printf after line 97, after line 104 and after line 106. in CanalOpen (https://github.com/grodansparadis/vscp_software/blob/master/src/vscp/drivers/level1/usb2can/usb2can/win32/usb2candrv.cpp) and we should see how it behave.

[2018-05-02T17:12:21Z | sjsf | comment]
While doing some manual testing, I realized that there is another potential source for wrong widget ID calculations: The `SitemapSubscriptionService` and the `SitemapProvider` both registered themselves as `ModelRepositoryChangeListener`s at the `ModelRepository`. The former uses the latter to get a cached instance of the model. 
There is no guarantee though about the order in which they get their `modelChanged()` methods called. So in case the `SitemapSubscriptionService` got called first, it used the stale widget copy given by the `SitemapProvider`, which can't know anything about the new model at this time. 
I have added a second commit which fixes this aspect by letting the `SitemapSubscriptionService` subscribe at the `SitemapProvider` for changes instead of the `ModelRepository` directly, thereby making sure it only gets notified when its trusted provider also knows about the change.

It looked into this and it seems that the default Spring MVC MultiPart implementation stores the file in memory. I consider this s bug, hawkBit should not use that implementation.

I will dig a bit further and see what we can do.

[2019-01-11T08:21:20Z | kaizimmerm | comment]
It seems that Jetty interprets Springs MultiPart config for file to disk as never instead of always. You can fix this by setting the property `spring.http.multipart.file-size-threshold=1MB` . We will make this the default with 0.3

Currently the payload size of the incoming messages are calculated and stored in the Prometheus server based on the configured minimum message size for each tenant. When a message is received from a device, the protocol adapter currently uses the payload size of that incoming message plus the data volume already used up by that tenant(from Prometheus server) to validate the message limit. Instead of using the actual payload size of the incoming message, a payload size should be derived based on the configured minimum message size and be used for the message limit validation. I will fix this.

[2017-09-18T13:32:11Z | graham-hanson | comment]
Hi @user2684,

You can enable compiler warnings in the Arduino IDE in File, Preferences - set Compiler Warnings to All.

You should fix the two "return-statement with no value" warnings - in these cases, the functions will return an undefined value (what the C++ standard calls "undefined behaviour" - meaning that you may sometimes get the expected effect but you may get a different effect each time you call the function and that includes sometime crashing the program completely!)

The problem with the line

    if (_sensors[sensor_index] != 0) _sensors[sensor_index] == 0;

which was originally just 

    _sensors[sensor_index] == 0;

is that it should simply be 

    _sensors[sensor_index] = nullptr; // Reset the pointer

i.e., an assignment rather than an equality test - very common mistake but it indicates the importance of using the highest level of warnings from the compiler!
(Note C++11 prefers use of the nullptr literal to zero as it can only be assigned to a pointer variable and is self documenting.)

Regards
Graham (also graham86 on MySensors forum)

[2017-10-02T08:06:31Z | graham-hanson | comment]
Hi Sergio,
The deprecated conversion warnings are because the code is assigning a string constant - `""` to a `char *` variable.
The problem is that a string constant has type `const char[]` so assigning to `char *` looses the `const`. (And also because the code could then attempt to write to the constant string, which, probably doesn't have enough space, may be shared with other pieces of code and may be in Read Only memory)
 
In this case, as all the member variables (3 of them from memory) causing this warning are assigned pointers to strings that are never updated, the variables should be declared as e.g.,

    const char * _value_string = "";

(To clarify, the strings assigned to the variables are never updated through the variable, but pointers to different strings are assigned to the variables.)

I have never come across as case where the compiler generates a warning for simply using a C-style cast in a C++ program instead of the C++ equivalent cast.  GCC will warning about certain conversions such as using `(char*)` to remove the constness from a `const char*`,  because it is dangerous.
The use of C-Style casts in a C++ program are not recommended as they, as in the example above, override some of the C++ language protections and result in "dangerous" code.

Finally, it is considered bad practice to ignore compiler warnings, even if .  Best practice is considered to be to compile with the highest warning level available and to "fix" all warnings.  In fact, the preferred method is to enable the compiler "Warnings are Errors" option (-Werror for the gcc compiler used for Arduino).  In practice, it can be difficult or impossible to remove all warnings, in particular because some my be generated by library code. However, the aim should be to reduce the number of warnings as far as possible, and for warnings in your "own" code to be reduced to zero.

This is due to the time format used in the custom date range dialog. Since it's in a M/d/yy (single-digit month/single digit day/two digit year, e.g. 01/25/18 for January 25th, 2018) it gets wrongly parsed to a Date object by `SimpleDateFormat`. According to the SimpleDateFormat JavaDoc:

> For parsing with the abbreviated year pattern ("y" or "yy"), SimpleDateFormat must interpret the abbreviated year relative to some century. It does this by adjusting dates to be within 80 years before and 20 years after the time the SimpleDateFormat instance is created. For example, using a pattern of "MM/dd/yy" and a SimpleDateFormat instance created on Jan 1, 1997, the string "01/11/12" would be interpreted as Jan 11, 2012 while the string "05/04/64" would be interpreted as May 4, 1964. During parsing, only strings consisting of exactly two digits, as defined by Character.isDigit(char), will be parsed into the default century. Any other numeric string, such as a one digit string, a three or more digit string, or a two digit string that isn't all digits (for example, "-1"), is interpreted literally. So "01/02/3" or "01/02/003" are parsed, using the same pattern, as Jan 2, 3 AD. Likewise, "01/02/-3" is parsed as Jan 2, 4 BC.

I propose to use a more explicit format for the year, using yyyy, and more in general to use the following format for the date and time, already used in Kapua in other sections: `dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm`

@stefanomorson what do you think?

[2019-04-30T20:17:11Z | trilokgm | comment]
> @trilokgm , the beehive core has a graceful shutdown method which does modules cleanup. When we call os.Exit(1), this would trigger the graceful shutdown right ? is this happening now ?

Beehive captures os signals and makes call which end up in context cleanup. The goroutines are not stopped in graceful shutdown call.

os.Exit(1) does not send any signal to invoke graceful shutdown execution flow. The program exits with an error code, here it is 1. There is no panic or stack trace generated.

I had given a thought about using uniform error codes, had to drop the idea due to significant usage of go routines without error notification.Due to this, there is not much significance seen for using error codes for now.

[2017-11-16T14:19:25Z | htreu | comment]
I did an analysis, this is a bug in ESH.

### Technical explanation
Two ItemProviders will try to add new items to the ItemRegistry: 
* The ChannelItemProvider will create "virtual" items for every ItemChannelLink it starts to handle. In case the link points to an item which is not already loaded and added to the ItemRegistry it will create one which lacks of cause all the meta information like label, groupNames, etc.
* The ManagedItemProvider will add all the items loaded from the storage service (here MapDB) to the ItemRegistry. Here all the items have the full meta information available.

Since https://github.com/eclipse/smarthome/pull/3670 there is a mechanism in the AbstractRegistry which prevents duplicate elements. This introduced also the behaviour we can see here: When the ChannelItemProvider is the first to add its items to the ItemRegistry the ManagedItemProvider will later try to add its items too and create the log messages.

### Workaround
In case all items in a setup are either provided by .items files or created vie PaperUI/REST API and not automagically by the ChannelItemProvider (which is needed primarily when activating new channels in PaperUI in "Simple Mode"*), the ChannelItemProvider can be deactivated completely. To achieve this create a `channelitemprovider.cfg` file with content `enabled=false` in the `conf/services` folder of the installation.

\* in Simple Mode no real items are created but only "virtual" items are implicitly created by the ChannelItemProvider.

@mherwege, do you mind testing the described workaround with your setup?

[2016-01-18T17:43:11Z | cdealti | comment]
> If I set the value of a service property to an empty string in the web UI and hit Apply the empty string is accepted and the corresponding service gets the empty string. 

If the configuration with an "empty" value is validated by the Web UI, it means that the `required` attribute of the property in the service metatype is set to false.
If the property has a default value in the metatype, the Kura `ConfigurationService` should pass this default to the service (a `ConfigurableComponent`). This is the behavior when Kura starts reading the configuration from the latest snapshot file but there is no configuration for the service. We say that we merge the configuration snapshot with the metatype defaults. 

> When KURA gets restarted the value reverts to the default value from the metatype file

We will make sure a configuration update through the Web UI will be merged with metatype defaults if needed.

About your use case, since you are working on a Windows port of Kura, I'm quite sure you don't want a metatype default for the **command.working.directory**. This is because Kura assumes there is only one metatype XML file matching the service pid.
In other words you can only have a single default value and in your case it won't work well both for Linux and Windows.

By removing the default from the metatype, the service will not receive the **command.working.directory** and can fallback using a default working directory which is suitable for every OS, for example the temporary directory through the Java property **java.io.tmpdir**.

If you are happy with this, please also update the property description in the metatype to describe what is the default working directory if it is not explicitly set.

void receive(const MyMessage &message)
{
  int childPin = message.sensor;
  //  Serial.println(message.getBool());


  for (int i = 0; i<iomodus_count; i++) ////search All Sensor Variables and set them
  {
    MyMessage msg(i, iomodus[i].variableType);
    while (iomodus[i].sensorType == S_UNUSED) { i++; }  //do not waste time to check UNUSED pins

                              //********************************IF VAR1 = Temp OFFSET existst*************************************** 
    if (message.type == V_VAR1)
    {
      if ((childPin == i) && (iomodus[i].sensorType == S_TEMP) && (iomodus[i].sensorVersion == "MAX31855"))
      {
        Temp_offset[i] = message.getFloat();
      }
    }
    if (message.type == V_VAR1)
    {
      if ((childPin == i) && (iomodus[i].sensorType == S_TEMP) && (iomodus[i].sensorVersion == "NTC"))
      {
        Temp_offset[i] = message.getFloat();
      }
    }
    //********************************IF VAR2 = LPF (Low Pass Filter existst*************************************** 
    if (message.type == V_VAR2)
    {
      //***************Low Pass Filter**************
      if ((childPin == i) && (iomodus[i].sensorType == S_TEMP) && (iomodus[i].sensorVersion == "MAX31855") && (message.getFloat() <= 1.0))
      {
        ktype_LPF_rate[i] = message.getFloat();
      }
    }
    //********************************IF V_STATUS or V_LIGHT existst*************************************** 
    if (message.type == V_STATUS)
    {
      if ((childPin == i) && (iomodus[i].sensorType == S_BINARY) && (iomodus[i].sensorVersion == "RELAY"))
      {
        if (relstate[i] != message.getBool())
        {
          digitalWrite(i, message.getBool() ? RELAY_ON : RELAY_OFF);
          relstate[i] = message.getBool();
          // Store state in eeprom
          saveState(i, message.getBool());
        }
      }
    }
    //********************************IF V_PERCENTAGE or V_DIMMER existst*************************************** 
    if ((childPin == i) && (message.type == V_PERCENTAGE) && (message.getInt() != last_int_value[i]))
    {
      Serial.println("im pwm");
      Serial.println(i);
      Serial.println(message.getInt());
      //***************PWM Rate 0 to 100 (%)**************  
      if ((childPin == i) && (iomodus[i].sensorVersion == "PWM") && (i <= 13))
      {
        Serial.println("im digital");
        pinMode(i, OUTPUT);
        analogWrite(i, message.getInt()*2.55); // Set Value 0-255
        last_int_value[i] = message.getInt();
      }
      //http://www.instructables.com/id/Analog-Output-Convert-PWM-to-Voltage/
      if ((childPin == i) && (iomodus[i].sensorVersion == "PWM_5V") && (i >= 54) && (i <= 69))
      {
        Serial.println("im analog");
        pinMode(i, OUTPUT);
        analogWrite(i, message.getInt()*2.55); // Set Value 0-255
        last_int_value[i] = message.getInt();
      }


    }


  }

[2016-07-25T13:55:46Z | ctron | comment]
This seems like a deadlock situation to me which is in the end "resolved" by running into a timeout. Maybe not properly cleaning up by that.

The `CamelCloudClient` is unsubscribing from topics and for this executing a call on the `CamelContext` inside a thread the executor of the `cloudClientExecutor` executor service. Which belongs to the `CamelContext`.

The other thread is the service itself, calling into the `CamelContext`, closing it, which is then closing all services, the executor service being one of those services, since it is shut down by using `shutdown`, waiting for all tasks (including the unsubscribe from above) to complete.

I think it should be sufficient to not use an executor service from Camel, but to simply maintain a plain `ExecutorService` from `newSingleThreadExecutor()`, disposing it during the `release` call.

[2017-08-08T05:43:15Z | czyba | comment]
Hi @ewertons,

I noticed this issue because I actually experienced the block in a program. Afterwards I checked the code to find out why it actually occurs. As far as I can see it is roughly because of this:

1. As you said, `IoTHubClient_UploadToBlobAsync` only blocks in order to create the thread. And indeed, that does not seem to be the issue.
2. The thread however runs the `uploadingThread` function, which in turn calls `Lock(savedData->iotHubClientHandle->LockHandle)`. During the period when the lock is being held `IoTHubClient_LL_UploadToBlob(savedData->iotHubClientHandle->IoTHubClientLLHandle, savedData->destinationFileName, savedData->source, savedData->size)` is called, which is a blocking call.
3. The `ScheduleWork_Thread` tries to lock the IoTHub before sending messages. Since the file upload still holds the lock for some time no message will be sent until the file upload is completed or aborted.

Furthermore since nearly all methods require to lock the IoTHub, so suddenly the async non-blocking calls and all other "immediate" calls will result in blocking operations. I have modified and attached the
[iothub_client_sample_upload_to_blob.c](https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/files/1206998/iothub_client_sample_upload_to_blob_c.txt) sample such that it exhibits said behavior. In my sample I have used SetRetryPolicy for simplicity sake, but the issue occurs with nearly all functions.

This also results in the IoTHub not being destroyed, since the file upload is not interrupted. Thus it may happen that a program may not terminate immediately but just in a couple of seconds if a file upload is in progress. I hope this showcases my issues.

Kind Regards,
Christopher Czyba

https://github.com/kubeedge/kubeedge/blob/be4d5e34012d41246919296ee378c1834b9ec097/edge/pkg/devicetwin/dtcontext/dtcontext.go#L131-L138

[2019-08-11T09:09:33Z | CoDanny | comment]
The key can be lost for many other reasons including expiration of credentials after not using it for a long time. This problem was about they key being forgotten repeatedly in a short amount of time. After consulting with a few affected users, this particular problem (there might be others) seems to have been solved. Two things were causing it:

1) A bug in our software by which a rejection of connection by our servers would log the user out. This sometimes meant that poor connectivity or misconfigured boxes (see second reason below) could wrongly log you our and ask you to log in again.

2) Users using an OctoPi devices which was made off a clone of another one were the plugin was active created a situation where two boxes were being logged into our system as one. When a box logs into our system with the same Box Id as another, the previous one is kicked out, this caused reason number 1 above happened.

This issues has now grown quite large and is confusing people that for other reasons loose their credentials on occasion to add comments here. I'm going to close and lock this issue now.

If you experience loss of credentials again, please reopen another ticket and explain how often this happens, look to see if you have more than one OctoPi connected to your account and whether the second one was a clone of the first and provide this info in the ticket.

The keys commands expects a `--protocol tcp` argument. So, not sure this is a bug other than missing documentation?

So the question is what to do when `--protocol` is not provided. Here's a few options:
- for devices with a single protocol, default to that (current behaviour on Core/Photon/P1)
- for devices with multiple protocol support:
  - raise an error if `--protocol` is not specified. This makes it clear there are multiple protocols and that the user needs to be clear which one they mean. (But this is inconvenient for the majority who never change from the default.)
  - a more friendly alternative -  inspect the device to determine the current protocol in use and default to that. Only raise the error above if for some reason the protocol cannot be determined.

The online/offline status works very well for LIFX lights. So if you want to know when the light was last online you can still use the transition from online to offline for this.
