[2016-12-08T23:25:11Z | damonbarry | comment]
Fixed with commit 00ab31f.

Metahost.h is available in several locations (and they're all the same for our purposes), e.g. on my dev box:

     C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\8.1\Include\um\metahost.h
     C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\NETFXSDK\4.6\Include\um\metahost.h
     C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\NETFXSDK\4.6.1\Include\um\metahost.h

Metahost.h is NOT available in the Windows 10 SDK for whatever reason. If you're targeting this SDK, I think it is expected that you'll pull it from the NETFX SDK instead. What's weird is that the NETFX SDK include path *IS* part of the INCLUDE env var, and INCLUDE *should* be searched by VC build, but apparently that's not happening here.

So the fix is to add %NETFXSDKDir%Include\um to the include directories in the dotnet and dotnet_static projects. The NETFXSDKDir environment variable is set in the VS Developer Command Prompt (and the MSBuild Command Prompt).

[2017-05-16T13:21:06Z | sjsf | comment]
I don't know. Just executing them, I guess? 😉 

The problem with these tests for sure is that they actually are integration tests, not only testing the binding, but indirectly also the complete ESH framework. That's why the are hit by asynchronous behavior, automated magic like autoupdate if item states, auto linking and all that. If some of these things change in a slight aspect (e.g. timing, implemented in a different way), then these tests also suffer.

I think if you want to really get rid of this stuff, then it would make sense to reduce the test scope to the binding itself, just making sure it uses the ESH APIs correctly. I.e. if you want to test if a certain action leads to an item update, just take the standalone ThingHandler, feed it with a mocked ThingHandlerCallback and ensure it's calling `stateUpdated(...)`. Don't care what happens afterwards. 

The new [testing documentation](https://github.com/eclipse/smarthome/blob/master/docs/documentation/development/testing.md#mockito) gives a pretty good example of how this can be done using plain Java 8 (hooray) with Mockito. For the majority of binding tests, this suffices and there is hardly any need for OSGiTests.

[2019-02-15T17:48:51Z | jspaith | comment]
You have GatewayHostname, but the correct value is GatewayHostName – note the capital ‘N’ in name.  This is why the argument is ignored and you’re always hitting the hub.

In the perfect world I’d make the client just fail if it doesn’t recognize a value, but thanks to back-compat I’m afraid to do that.  We could argue whether it should be a stricmp() instead of strcmp(), but again my fear would be someone did what you’re doing and has a happily working system of ‘n’, not ‘N’. And then they push updated SDK and we accept the ‘n’ and it turns out the gateway all of a sudden we start parsing is bogus and breaks stuff.

I think what we should do though is LogError() when we don’t recognize output (along with a note that the error is going to be ignored and we'll keep on parsing).

If anyone in community has any thoughts, feel free to jump onto this thread.

Yes this is a **Docker Hub** Automated Build limitation of trying to produce automated Documentation for user using the same mechanism as creating an automated branch build for testing.

What I think you're actually after is the `SOURCE_BRANCH` **Env** variable which is currently only available in **Docker Cloud.**

The current approach defaults to latest `master` because that is the **branch**  hard-coded in the Dockerfile
https://github.com/telefonicaid/iotagent-ul/blob/770f3a2a77e652e51b1cf275ed97d581d92d9c9b/docker/Dockerfile#L53-L55 

You have several options here:

1) Within the `Dockerfile` line 55 replace `master` with a specific hash
* https://github.com/telefonicaid/iotagent-ul/archive/2120915c9be82fa8fcee55c2d824a39e9a082c4a.zip

2) Within the `Dockerfile` line 55 replace `master` with the name of the branch you are using:
* https://github.com/telefonicaid/iotagent-ul/archive/task/keyrockOauth2Integration-prelanding.zip

3) Build locally using a copied `Dockerfile` and replace the `RUN` statement with a `COPY`

[2019-12-21T09:12:47Z | petergebruers | comment]
I think it worth pointing out that OZW 1.6, in general, "auto clears" these values:
Scene Activation
Central Scene
Alarm aka Notification

When one of those events are reported by the device, OZW will change the value to indicate it got triggered. Then, after some time OZW will clear that value.

So In the log you first see the button press or alarm, then after some time:

""Automatically Clearing Scene" if it is Central Scene
""Automatically Clearing SceneID/Duration in" if it is Scene Activation
""Automatically Clearing Alarm in %dms"" if is an Alarm (Notificaton)

In case of the Alarm, the situation is more complex than the Scene classes and here is a separate discussion about that:

https://github.com/OpenZWave/open-zwave/issues/1889 "COMMAND_CLASS_ALARM "magic" clear issue"

[2019-01-07T20:34:15Z | YoDaMa | comment]
Good to hear you managed the problem! As to your question, let me give it a crack. 

The difference between the two comes down to the fact that in particular with the AMQP protocol you have the option to use multiplexing through the transport to weave the data of multiple so-called 'Devices' through a single communication point. So a device handle will point to a struct that has information related to a 'Device'. A transport handle will point to a struct that has information related to the transport (AMQP).

To your question of why would subscribe use the device handle and unsubscribe use the transport handle, the question must be understood through the context of *where* the calls are being made. 

In `IoTHubClientCore_LL_SetDeviceMethodCallback` both calls for subscribe and unsubscribe are made using the device handle. This makes sense since we are calling into `IoTHubTransport_Subscribe`, which in AMQP takes in a device handle to subscribe that device to method callbacks (it doesn't make sense if you are multiplexing to use a transport handle to subscribe a single device to a method callback). 

In `iothubtransportamqp_methods_subscribe` we are just adjusting the device state to indicate that it needs to subscribe to methods. During the transport's DoWork call, it will check for this device state and if indicated it will update the transport by calling into `_iothubtransportamqp_methods_unsubscribe` which will unsubscribe the device via the transport method handle. 

Hopefully this explanation is helpful! If I didn't explain it well enough or answer your question don't be shy.

[2017-07-25T12:30:00Z | htreu | comment]
Hi @aounhaider1, thanks for the review. The effect you see is actually the main drawback this refactoring introduces. In fact the thing-types do get cached. Unfortunately when rendering for the first time all things are rendered simultaneously and thing-types are requested multiple times. The cache is then filled during promise resolving but after (read: later) all thing-types have been requested.
In contrast to the angularjs digest cycle (which is responsible for nearly half the rendering time) the duplicate requests are really fast. Thats the reason I decided to live with this drawback (at least for now).

      state_template: '{{ "off" if value_json.value == 0 else "on" }}',

[2018-01-22T07:56:35Z | htreu | comment]
This is the result from my analysis:
* `PersistentInbox` will pass a newly discovered thing to the `thingAdded` method from the `AutomaticInboxProcessor` which does the `autoIgnore` check.
* the `AutomaticInboxProcessor` will call `setFlag(thingUID, IGNORED)` on the `PersistentInbox`. This marks the discovery result from the storage with the flag, not the instance which is currently processed by the `PersistentInbox`.
* `setFlag` will immediately post an `updated` event for the discovery result (note: this happens before an `added` event is emitted).
* Paper UI will happily ignore the `updated` event since no entry for the given thingUID is present in the Paper UI inbox repository.
* `PersistentInbox` will then post an `added` event with the instance the discovery service created. This instance does not have the `IGNORED` flag set.
* Paper UI will pick up the `added` event and display the discovery result as a new result, just because the flag is still set to `NEW`.

A refresh of the Paper UI inbox will retrieve all discovery results from the backend. Since the `IGNORED` flag was correctly set to the instance from the storage Paper UI will then correctly hide the auto-ignored result.

[2018-01-22T07:59:06Z | htreu | comment]
One solution would be to reload the discovered result from storage before emitting the first `add` event. This will then provide the correct flag.
The unused `updated` event is obsolete (in this scenario) but does not hurt as long as the client checks for existence of the given thingUID.

> mybe just a logging delay?

might indeed be the case. On the other hand, the scheduler just works on granularity of seconds, so it tries to schedule those two events for the identical time. And as these are independently scheduled events, we also get some fuzziness which naturally comes with multi threaded/parallel execution. Therefore it might not only be the logging, it actually also could be just coincidence. 

Therefore I suggest to further improve the astro binding to add a delay of at least one second to the end events in case start and end are to be scheduled "at the same time". I suppose such a small delay hurts us much less than the consequences in rules when the order is screwed up.

The package names and versions shown in the packages view are the name inside the `.dp` package. 
The name and version provided when installing is the reference name that you'll use if you run the installing in two step (first download and then install), because Kura uses that name to save the file. On receiving the `install` command, Kura looks at the available packages and search for the provided name and version. If it founds any matching it'll install it right away. 

Actually I think this should be managed more on the Kura side, which can eventually override the package name and version with the one that it receives from the platform.

[2018-09-06T20:32:50Z | RobertLucian | comment]
@deadprogram: When I had done my round of testing for the GrovePi with this firmware `v1.3.0`, I was able to poll the analog input ports simultaneously just fine, which means there has got to be something incompatible in your implementation.

I'm making 2 assumptions:
1. You implemented the API according to this version of the firmware and not the old one which had lots of bugs and which is not compatible with this one.
1. You're polling the ports in a single thread/process. The communication between the Pi and the GrovePi still isn't thread-safe and it won't be in the foreseeable future.

If both of my assumptions are correct, then I'm not sure what could be wrong with your implementation. Still, I could test the GrovePi again and see if polling multiple analog sensors continuously works - just to be 100% sure.

[2018-09-06T21:22:00Z | deadprogram | comment]
Hi @RobertLucian thank you for the quick response. 

Both of your assumptions are mostly correct. Firstly, yes, this is the 1.3.0 API. Second, even though there are 2 goroutines, access to the i2c bus on the *host* is synced. However, after looking closer at the driver, it was not really synchronous enough when talking to the GrovePi as a device. You mentioning the threading was the clue. I added an additional mutex to control "transactionality" of the communication with the GrovePi, and now it is responding as expected.

Thanks again!

In many asynchronous calls (connect, disconnect, publish, subscribe), the client library is currently using `waitForCompletion()` without specifying a timeout value.   Therefore, the calling thread will block and may not return to the caller.

The fix is to add a new global property named `"ActionTimeout"`, in milliseconds which can be set by the application when instantiating the IoT client objects.  If the `"ActionTimeout"` property is not specified, the default timeout is 30 seconds.

Also new methods with a `timeout` parameter will be added for publishing/subscribing events and command.

Another possible solution: 
Use only `(assert, $deviceId)` as cache key in `RegistrationClientImpl.assertRegistration`.
When having a cache hit, check the cache value and the `last-via` gateway id in it. If it differs from the gateway id used in the request, retrieve the current registration information from the RegistrationService and update the cache entry.

[2019-03-21T10:16:47Z | BobClaerhout | comment]
I'm not familiar with the assertRegistration but if it can be compared with a database table I think I would create a table where the DeviceId would be the primary key of that table. If this assumption is correct, I would rather go for the second solution.
On the other hand: is it really needed to check if the id is the same, can't you  just always update the cache entry or is the update an expensive operation?

[2019-03-21T10:50:31Z | calohmn | comment]
Yes, the second solution is probably more straightforward.

> is it really needed to check if the id is the same, can't you just always update the cache entry or is the update an expensive operation?

Updating the cache entry is not enough, we have to do the remote call to the Registration Service and have the `last-via` property be updated in the device registry that way.
In order not to do that unnecessarily, the gateway id is checked. At least that was my initial idea.

But, thinking further about this, for devices with multiple `via` entries, I think we **always** have to do the remote call and update the `last-via` property in the device registry, because there could be multiple protocol adapter instances involved.
An example:
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-1` to protocol adapter instance `http-1` => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to `gw-1`
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-2` to _another_ protocol adapter instance `http-2` => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to `gw-2`
- device `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-1` to protocol adapter instance `http-1` => regardless of cache content, remote call has to be done in order to set last-via to `gw-1`

[2019-03-21T11:17:21Z | BobClaerhout | comment]
> An example:
> 
> - device dev-A connects via gateway gw-1 to protocol adapter instance http-1 => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to gw-1
> - device dev-A connects via gateway gw-2 to another protocol adapter instance http-2 => no cache hit, assertRegistration is invoked, last-via is set to gw-2
> - device dev-A connects via gateway gw-1 to protocol adapter instance http-1 => regardless of cache content, remote call has to be done in order to set last-via to gw-1

I think you have to assume that your cache is always out of sync. At the second action, `dev-A` connects via gateway `gw-2` you will have to perform a remote call as well. I think the local cache is a rather dangerous concept in this case. The master of this data should be the device registry (and there will always be just one device registry, if not a syncing mechanism should be added here as well). So I propose to always request the data from the device registry and update the data in the device registry instead of keeping a local cache. This does not have to block the normal flow as it can be updated after the telemetry or event data is sent to the AMQP broker.

[2019-03-21T13:01:03Z | sophokles73 | comment]
The device registry implementation can control the caching behavior in the adapters by means of the *caching policy* which is included in all responses to *assert Registration*. The registry could, e.g. use the *no cache* policy for devices that are allowed to connect via multiple gateways and use the normal cache policy for devices that are only allowed to connect via a single gateway (or none at all).

[2019-06-10T21:03:41Z | wborn | comment]
The issue is that `SerialPortUtil` sets the environment variable `gnu.io.rxtx.SerialPorts` to a value when it's not set:

https://github.com/openhab/openhab-core/blob/7f5ceefa26ffdf6ea290c9717868814b6318ff13/bundles/org.openhab.core.io.transport.serial.rxtx/src/main/java/org/eclipse/smarthome/io/transport/serial/internal/SerialPortUtil.java#L44

After that, whenever nrjavaserial is used to get the serial port identifiers (`CommPortIdentifier.getPortIdentifiers()`), it will only return the ports set in that environment variable (see [nrjavaserial code](https://github.com/NeuronRobotics/nrjavaserial/blob/e06ed10e23284c36d19225b907e0b7a3b2736833/src/main/java/gnu/io/RXTXCommDriver.java#L418-L422)). So maybe it can be fixed by making sure the environment variable is restored to its original value after using it for creating the `SerialPortIdentifierImpl`?

https://github.com/openhab/openhab-core/blob/7f5ceefa26ffdf6ea290c9717868814b6318ff13/bundles/org.openhab.core.io.transport.serial.rxtx/src/main/java/org/eclipse/smarthome/io/transport/serial/internal/RxTxPortProvider.java#L49-L58

[2018-11-28T21:42:43Z | jebrando | comment]
@larsonmpdx you hit a quirk with the gcc compiler, I'll try to explain (very poorly) below.  Moving the umqtt lib above aziotsharedutil will fix the issue and we shall fix our documentation to make it more clear.  Your target_link_libraries code should look like this:

target_link_libraries(myproject
        iothub_client
        iothub_client_mqtt_transport
        umqtt
        uhttp
        aziotsharedutil
        pthread
        curl
        ssl
        crypto
        m
          # shouldn't be needed. see issue https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-sdk-c/issues/550
	  # prov_auth_client # causes conflicts on source-built sdk, nov 2018
	  # hsm_security_client # causes conflicts on source-built sdk, nov 2018
        uuid
        parson
        )

The reason this error occurred is that gcc gathers the dependencies as it goes along from top to bottom if a dependency is encountered of a library that has been previously scanned, the code won't be found, generating a undefined reference error.  The StringToken_Split is a new function and this is the first release where it's been used and it's only being used in umqtt.  Since no other library above the aziotsharedutil is using that function when gcc get to that library it discards that function to save space, not knowing that later on umqtt will need this function.

Let me know if you have any more question on this.

### Fingerprint

Adding a TLS fingerprint effectively pins the device to a particular certificate. Furthermore, as currently implemented by _WifiSecureClient()_, both `mqtt.host` and `ota.host` are verified against the server certificate's common name (`CN`) in the certificate subject or in the SANs (subjectAlternateName) contained in it, but not in their IP addresses. So, if the certificate used by your server looks like

```
Subject: CN=tiggr.example.org, OU=generate-CA/emailAddress=nobody@example.net
...
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
  IP Address:192.168.1.10, DNS:broker.example.org
```

enabling fingerprint in Homie will work only if `host` is set to `tiggr.example.org` or `broker.example.org` _and_ the correct fingerprint is used; setting `host` to the IP address will cause fingerprint verification to fail.

[2017-06-29T20:00:20Z | ohinckel | comment]
> 2017-04-30 00:50:01 WARNING Sml Skipping unkown field 0x47

The type 0x47 indicates a boolean value which has usually only one byte value and should be declared as 0x42 and not 0x47. Maybe this error happens since the data stream contains errors, or the parsing failed completely (e.g. when trying to parse entities while one byte shifted).

> 2017-04-30 00:50:01 WARNING Sml Can not parse entity at position 4225, byte 14: can't multiply sequence by non-int of type 'float': 77 07 01 00 01 08 01 ff 01 01 62 1e 52 ff 00 55 05 55 33 b6 01 77 07 b2 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0...

This seems to be a reading error, since the end of stream contains too much `00` values. Do you have problem reading from your device? Maybe the cable is too long or the power supply too small?

> 2017-04-30 01:21:07 WARNING Sml Can not parse entity at position 4095, byte 9: unsupported operand type(s) for ** or pow(): 'int' and 'bytes': 77 07 81 81 c7 82 03 ff 01 00 01 01 01 04 48 48 41 47

Packet analysis: OBIS Code `81 81 c7 82 03 ff`,
* followed by `01` for `objName` (optional, empty)
* followed by `00` for `status` (optional, empty)
* followed by `01` for `valTime` (optional, empty)
* followed by `01` for `unit` (optional, empty)
* followed by `01` for `scaler` (optional, empty)
* followed by `04` for `value` (optional, 3 byte octet data `48 41 47`)

The expression to fail in [SML plugin](https://github.com/smarthomeNG/plugins/blob/042b451bbc04d650bd88ca48aade9bb46eb29c82/sml/__init__.py#L232) is
`entry['value'] * 10 ** entry['scaler'] if entry['scaler'] is not None else entry['value']`
But the `scaler` value should be `None` and no `pow` call should be done. Maybe the operator precedence is playing with us and rewriting the line to the following should clarify:
`(entry['value'] * 10 ** entry['scaler']) if entry['scaler'] is not None else entry['value']`

I start fixing some issues in the SML plugin and wrote some tests. If you want you can try by [branch](https://github.com/ohinckel/smarthomeNG-plugins/tree/issue-201).

To verify and be able to fix other problems please provide the SML data (logged in Debug mode). I'll take care to look into it and write some tests for this.

Attempting to close the client handle while MQTT over websockets is continuously trying to reconnect on failed MQTT ping.

[2019-04-01T18:51:09Z | maskimthedog | comment]
I am using the LL calls on a single thread.

[2019-04-01T18:51:54Z | maskimthedog | comment]

[2019-04-16T19:31:23Z | maskimthedog | comment]
I believe what is happening is this...

MQTT connection is active and a ping failure occurs because of a signal disruption.
Then transport_data->currPacketState != DISCONNECT_TYPE when DisconnectFromClient() is called the transport is freed and transport_data->currPacketState is set to DISCONNECT_TYPE within the function.
Next the SDK attempts to reconnect calling InitializeConnection() which calls ResetConnectionIfNecessary() freeing up the transport (if a connection attempt has been made previously) prior to calling SendMqttConnectMsg() which calls GetTransportProviderIfNecessary() to allocate the transport.
This all plays well until IoTHubTransport_MQTT_Common_Destroy() is called which calls DisconnectFromClient().  Since transport_data->currPacketState is still set to DISCONNECT_TYPE, DisconnectFromClient() does not free the transport.

[2019-08-28T19:21:35Z | jspaith | comment]
@maskimthedog - agree with your analysis of this.  I think a safer fix here though is to add in `free_transport_handle_data` logic the `xio_destroy(transport_data->xioTransport)` call.   

`free_transport_handle_data` acts as the "destructor" of the handle.  So by putting the `xio_destroy` call here we make sure that any code path - now or future - does not have to rely on `DisconnectFromClient` being in just the right state first.  

Also the `if (transport_data->currPacketState != DISCONNECT_TYPE)` in disconnect does provide a useful service of making sure we don't send multiple disconnect packets to server.  So I'd rather leave that alone.

I've reviewed code and don't see other such leaks.  For something of this severity though I'll need further consultation with my colleagues.  If you have any concerns with my fix please let me know as you've obviously gone quite deep into this code.

Thanks for your excellent analysis on this and to echo @rafilho apologies on delays here.

When the GenericItemProvider reads the fixed items file in, it first creates the links (and adds the items later, be it the correct strategy or not - I think we can optimize this, but that's another story...). So the ChannelItemProvider gets notified about those updates [here](https://github.com/eclipse/smarthome/blob/3ae5d7b1b284f2bde6199bfe8dad950fd38cae39/bundles/core/org.eclipse.smarthome.core.thing/src/main/java/org/eclipse/smarthome/core/thing/internal/ChannelItemProvider.java#L315).

It then first removes the item from the `items` map and then informs its listeners (i.e. the registry) about it. The registry again informs _its_ listeners which happens to also be the ChannelItemProvider again, so it creates the item again (remember, the GenericItemProvider did not yet announce its model-items) and adds it correctly to the `items` map. When this notification chain returns to the first place, it _again_ removes the item from the map. So it lost track of it, but the registry still has it. 

When I remove the second `items.remove(key)` it suddenly behaves well again. So now I will "only" have to figure out why it was in there, if it really is an accident or if it by chance works around another bug.

[2017-06-10T19:58:46Z | sjsf | comment]
As you wanted to be kept updated: I just started writing test-cases for this issue and by doing so I understood a little more about the mechanism.

It actually needs three things to cause this issue: 

* The GenericItemChannelLinkProvider has some amnesia. It clears its context map, so it doesn't properly remember what it created/provided before. It needs an even number of updates, before a model removal can cause this issue (so it's not a heisenbug, it's just a 50% chance). Because of this amnesia, the ItemChannelLinks remain in the registry, therefore the ChannelItemProvider kicks in an creates the excess items. 
* As said before, the ChannelItemProvider has a built-in amnesia due to the internal-remove/inform-and-thereby-recreate/internal-remove sequence which makes it impossible for it to remove its own item later on when the model gets loaded again (I have described this above). It just didn't surface so far because items from other providers seldomly come and go all the time.
* The question is why the ChannelItemProvider is part of this game at all... As the links for model items actually also come from the model, it actually should not need to. It would me much more clever of the GenericItemProvider if it would _first_ create the items and _then_ create the links (and vice versa for deletion) so that the ChannelLinkProvider will not need to become active at all. This I think is the root-cause for the long outstanding, somehow mysterious #2491, which is very annoying for all bindings which do something "expensive" stuff whenever a channel gets linked.

I prepared two commit to fix all this already, but as I said yesterday, I will need a bit more time to thoroughly test it before I create PRs for them.

[2017-01-31T18:47:19Z | avranju | comment]
The issue here was that when you switched the build configuration to *Release* in Visual Studio for the gateway, it continued to link with the *Debug* build of the dependencies that it automatically built for you when you ran cmake. This is bad because on Windows, one gets different implementations of the C runtime (CRT) with different build configurations which means that anytime we have memory allocations and frees mixed between different CRTs, chaos ensues. A comprehensive fix for this issue will require us to change how we deal with gateway dependencies. We will essentially need to switch to depending on packages from external repositories such as *nuget* and *Aptitude*. This will take somewhat longer to accomplish and is on our backlog.

In the meantime we have checked in a change (https://github.com/Azure/azure-iot-gateway-sdk/commit/655cd7cb72d1c084f20c10732c21f9b1bddab587) that enables the following:

  - Propagate build configuration while automatically building dependencies when you run cmake, i.e., now when you run cmake you can pass the build configuration via the `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` cmake variable and it's value will be used as the configuration to use when building dependencies.
  - Support *rebuilding* of dependencies when running the build script (`build.cmd` or `build.sh`). This is necessary when you are *switching* configurations. For example,  you may have been working with the *Debug* configuration and would now like to build *Release* bits. In order to accomplish this you can now run the build script like so -
    ```
    build.cmd --rebuild-deps --config Release
    ```
  - Enable generation of debug symbols for all release configurations on Windows

This should hopefully unblock you.

[2016-09-15T09:31:46Z | cdealti | comment]
@dwoodard1 The root cause of this is that the `org.eclipse.iot.greenhouse.publisher.GreenhousePublisher` component has `configuration-policy = optional`. This is perfectly legal but it's not common for a Kura `ConfigurableComponent`.

This is a regression introduced with Kura 2.0.0.
The problem is that the Kura `ConfigurationServiceImpl` assumes that the property `kura.service.pid` introduced with Kura 2.0.0 is always present.

If this property is not set in the component definition the `ComponentMetatypeBundleTracker` will set it to the value of `service.pid` and will update the component configuration.
If the component has `configuration-policy = required` it will become satisfied and it will activate with `kura.service.pid` properly set and `ConfigurationServiceImpl` will properly track it.

Otherwise, If the component has `configuration-policy = optional`, the component might activate before its configuration is updated by `ComponentMetatypeBundleTracker`. The ConfigurationServiceImpl will not find `kura.service.pid` ignoring the component and printing a warning:

```
2016-09-08 19:11:15,562 [Component Resolve Thread (Bundle 7)] WARN o.e.k.c.c.ConfigurationServiceImpl - Either kura.service.pid null or service.pid org.eclipse.iot.greenhouse.publisher.GreenhousePublisher are null
```

There are two workarounds:
1. In the `org.eclipse.iot.greenhouse.publisher.GreenhousePublisher` component definition set `configuration-policy = required`
2. In the `org.eclipse.iot.greenhouse.publisher.GreenhousePublisher` component definition add a new `kura.service.pid` and set it to  `org.eclipse.iot.greenhouse.publisher.GreenhousePublisher`

[2017-03-28T01:02:59Z | m-mcgowan | comment]
## Internal Design

- The partial Arduino API as it was in 0.6.0 is defined in `spark_wiring_arduino.h`. This file has been restored to it's former 0.6.0 state without the new Arduino APIs. This file is always included with Particle.h/application.h. 

- The full Arduino API is declared in "Arduino.h". By keeping it separate we make a clear distinction between which symbols are included in the partial API and the full API. 

- There is some overlap of the partial API and the full API - `constrain` and `range` are examples. In the partial API, these are declared as templates. In the full API, they are macros. Hence, the usual trick of using `#ifndef constrain` won't work in the full API since it's defined as a template and not a macro. The workaround is to use `PARTICLE_WIRING_ARDUINO_TEMPLATE` as a define when these few common symbols have already been defined in the partial API, so they are not re-defined in the full API.  If we are splitting hairs, this may mean that some arduino libraries fail to compile in cases where the template does not behave the same as the macro (or that they are relying upon double-evaluation side-effects of the macro!!).  In this rare (hopefully non-existent) case, it is possible to get the arduino version of these defines, by disabling the preprocessor, and including `Arduino.h` at the top of the sketch.

[2017-04-05T15:12:07Z | m-mcgowan | comment]
Once the arduino header is included, the symbols remain visible until the end of the compilation unit (and for all subsequent headers.)

For example, in this case 

```
#include "libraryExpecting062ArduinoSymbols.h"  // library 1
#include "libraryExpecting060Symbols.h"  // library 2
```

The second library is not expecting the arduino symbols to be defined (e.g. it might declare it's own copy of `SPISettings`) but these symbols are defined if library 1 includes `Arduino.h` in its header. To work around this, includes should be done in libraries an applications in a way thats all the headers not expecting arduino support first, and then all arduino-dependent headers afterwards.  

In the example above, reversing the order of the headers would fix the problem.

[2015-10-24T21:50:22Z | mdolbin | comment]
I think we should not make Content-Type header optional for the number of reasons.

First of all it's not about having a some header string in a request. We need to explicitly check that sender wants to send exactly JSON string before we even try to parse it. 

For example, default Content-Type for POST request is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` which is used to send serialized HTML forms data. This means that the following code will produce the following payload: `command=command&parameters[prop1]=val1&parameters[prop2]=val2&parameters[prop3]=etc` which will cause JSON parsing error (assuming we are accepting all requests) on server-side and unexpected 500 Internal Server Error instead of code 415 with user-friendly error message:

```
$.ajax({
    type: "POST",
    url: "http://127.0.0.1:8080/dh/rest/device/e50d6085-2aba-48e9-b1c3-73c673e414be/command",
    headers: {"Authorization": "Bearer 1jwKgLYi/CdfBTI9KByfYxwyQ6HUIEfnGSgakdpFjgk="},
    data: {
        "command": "command",
        "parameters": {
            "prop1": "val1",
            "prop2": "val2",
            "prop3": "etc"
        }
    }
});
```

Sticking to standards also makes it easier for us to integrate with new tools, libraries and applications.

On the other hand, it's a good idea to transfer less bandwidth. For example, we can return 415 code on parsing error. 

@demon-xxi @zubrabubra @SorJEF What do you think? Let's discuss and make some decision regarding this issue.

[2015-10-26T16:38:09Z | zubrabubra | comment]
I would go with defaulting content type to application json and then making it the only choice for now.  What are the reasons device would decide to send us data form encoded?

As from device perspective both json and form encoded are not native, while json accepted by human beings easily, and when someone looks on `command=command&parameters[prop1]=val1&parameters[prop2]=val2&parameters[prop3]=etc` he become disappointed with a fact that he needs to catch symbols in this spagetti :)

[2018-05-01T09:15:35Z | cgawron | comment]
I ran into the same issue.  The reason seems to be that the code assumes that the message length is 16 bit long at maximum, e.g. here
```
const char* mqtt_get_publish_topic(uint8_t* buffer, uint16_t* length);
const char* mqtt_get_publish_data(uint8_t* buffer, uint16_t* length);
```
and in deliver_publish as well (mqtt_data_len, mqtt_offset are declared as uint16_t). My firmware has more than 64k length, so there is a overrun.

Another point is that the the topic is only set in the first event - I needed to adapt my callback accordingly. Maybe this should be documented or changed - the callback is easier to implement if the topic is present in every event structure.

[2018-05-01T18:28:52Z | cgawron | comment]

Thank you for providing espmqtt!

[2018-05-02T20:09:58Z | cgawron | comment]
@DavidAntliff I hope that - apart from handling messages larger than 64k - this patch also fixes receiving multiple messages within one packet and messages spread over several packets.

Be aware that you will receive several events for large messages and only the first one contains the topic. Events having non-zero `current_data_offset` will contain no topic.

I've reread my statement and I admit I took a few shortcuts and it does not convey my message well... Sorry about that, let me try again...

The origin of the config files should match the version of OZW, when you build product X from source and that source is based on "master" you'll have OZW 1.6 with matching file.

Likewise, you could still check out the "1.4" branch (of the canonical repository) and build the OZW library and use the "config" subfolder - still everything will match.

Trouble starts when users come from another system and start copying over config files... Which is why I've mentioned the HASS situation, it applies to the Z-Wave Integration that has existed for several years now. If users install that Z-Wave part, it will pull in a fork of "pyozw" and that one in turn builds OZW (1.4-ish because it is a fork) from <https://github.com/home-assistant/open-zwave> - So when users start copying files around trouble indeed may start. Now OZW 1.6 also has that "revision" tag and fetches updates from a server that uses the "master" config files, something the 1.4 build does not do.

On my main system (a Mac) I debug and test doing "make install" and many of my (test) programs get their files from the system location. OZW 1.6 will tell you that, eg

```
Loading Localization File /usr/local/etc/openzwave/Localization.xml With Revision 8
```

Hass users, especially when they run the "docker" variants, might have set an explicit directory with a copy of the config dir, fo example to add a device.

Although the "Z-Wave Integration" does not have anything to do with Zwave2Mqtt I think it is best to be aware of this situation, I am sometimes active on their Z-Wave Discord channel and from time to time people talk about moving, migrating and copying stuff between systems and also between the Integration and Zwave2Mqtt

According to the OSGi spec a bundle/fragment is updated OSGi performs a refresh (stop and restart) of the bundles in its _dependency closure_. The dependency closure contains the list of bundles that directly or indirectly "depend" on the bundles being updated, and is obtainable using the `FrameworkWiring.getDependencyClosure()` method. The dependency closures of the bundles included in the `org.eclipse.kura.script.filter` dp are the following:

```
10:52:22,936 [Component Resolve Thread] INFO  ScriptFilter:90  - script filter dependency closure:
[org.eclipse.kura.wire.script.filter.provider_1.0.100.qualifier [40]]
10:52:22,936 [Component Resolve Thread] INFO  ScriptFilter:92  - localization bundle dependency closure: 
[org.eclipse.kura.wire.devel.component.provider_1.0.4.qualifier [134],
org.eclipse.kura.json.marshaller.unmarshaller.provider_1.0.0.qualifier [116],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.s7plc.provider_1.0.100.qualifier [74],
org.eclipse.kura.asset.helper.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [109],
org.eclipse.kura.localization_1.0.200.qualifier [85],
org.eclipse.kura.core.deployment_1.1.300.qualifier [10],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.gpio.localization_1.0.0.qualifier [119],
org.eclipse.kura.asset.provider_2.0.0.qualifier [45],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.script.filter.provider_1.0.100.qualifier [40],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.helper.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [33],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.gpio.provider_1.0.0.qualifier [56],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.opcua.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [126],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.s7plc.localization_1.0.100.qualifier [100],
org.eclipse.kura.web2_2.0.300.qualifier [76],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.component.join.provider_1.0.0.qualifier [11],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.component.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [37],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.helper.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [78],
org.eclipse.kura.xml.marshaller.unmarshaller.provider_1.0.0.qualifier [34],
org.eclipse.kura.driver.opcua.localization_1.0.200.qualifier [99],
org.eclipse.kura.util_1.0.200.qualifier [17],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.h2db.component.provider_1.0.100.qualifier [124],
org.eclipse.kura.camel.cloud.factory_1.1.200.qualifier [89],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.script.filter.localization_1.0.100.qualifier [29],
org.eclipse.kura.core.configuration_2.0.0.qualifier [97],
org.eclipse.kura.wire.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [5],
org.eclipse.kura.localization.resources_1.0.200.qualifier [42],
org.eclipse.kura.asset.cloudlet.provider_1.0.200.qualifier [130]]
```

The rules for computing the dependency closure are explained in the OSGi spec. Roughly speaking in this case the following should happen:
* Since the `org.eclipse.kura.wire.script.filter.localization` fragment is going to be updated, its host, 
`org.eclipse.kura.localization` belongs to the dependency closure.
* If a bundle A imports a package from bundle B that belongs to the dependency closure, then A belongs to the dependency closure as well.

`org.eclipse.kura.core.configuration` is in the closure because it imports the  `org.eclipse.kura.core.util` package from the `org.eclipse.kura.util` bundle, which in turn imports the `org.eclipse.kura.localization`package.

This should also explain why the Web Ui is restarted in scenario shown in issue #1689.

[2019-10-02T20:42:42Z | mkellsy | comment]
I found the issue. In the past our upgrade process required the --ignore-scripts flag on the npm install. This flag is preventing the post upgrade scripts from running.

I have published 3.0.0-beta.62 to address this, with a failsafe in case the upgrade script is not ran.

If you already upgraded to beta 60 or 61. You can try to access the interface at http://hoobs.local:51827. Then click Check for Updates and update to beta 62. After the upgrade you should be able to access the interface at http://hoobs.local.

If you are unable to access the interface or unable to log in (the bug beta.60 was trying to fix). You need to access the terminal via SSH.

1. Open a terminal from Mac, or Putty on Windows.
2a. On mac type `ssh hoobs@hoobs.local` the password is **hoobsadmin**
2b. On Putty on Windows, set the Host **hoobs.local**, and the port to **22**. Click **Open**.
2b. Then enter **hoobs** for the username and **hoobsadmin** for the password.
3. Now run this command `sudo npm install -g --unsafe-perm @hoobs/hoobs` and wait for it to finish.
4. Then run `sudo reboot`

After the device reboots, the interface should appear.

[2017-02-27T23:53:42Z | erkkah | comment]
@owenwaller, the layer in `drivers/i2c` does two things, first it adds support for i2c on platforms that do not have sysfs, currently the firmata has it's own implementation. Second, it makes it possible to support several different i2c buses at the same time in a consistent manner.

In the sysfs case, it acts as a proxy on top of `sysfs/i2c_device.go`, so you are right that the interfaces are duplicated.

The general idea of the chosen set of methods is to make it easy to follow datasheets and preexisting example code. WriteBlockData happens to be part of the SMBus lingo, and is always limited to 32 bytes. For a pure SMBus device, it is not possible to use `Write()` with bigger blocks.

The challenge with implementing `ReadBlockData()` using `Read()` is to write the register/command byte to the device before reading. Some devices will accept setting the register/command by a single byte write before reading. If that is not accepted, `Read()` will always start from register 0, so even if you want to read from regs 5 to 15 you would have to read the first 5 and throw away the result.

Because of this, I think it is safe to leave `ReadBlockData()` out.

[2018-07-10T11:47:02Z | sophokles73 | comment]
The problem seems to be that we *switch* the vert.x `Context` while processing requests. When a request comes in it is handled on the event loop context that has been created when the HTTP adapter verticle gets deployed. This Context is associated with one of the event loop threads, say *event-loop-thread-0*.

When Spring instantiates the HonoClient instances for connecting to the registry and AMQP network, these instances all create a new vert.x Context to run on in their constructor. So, let's say the client for accessing the Tenant service runs on a Context that is associated with *event-loop-thread-1*.

Now, when an HTTP request is being processed, we first try to authenticate the device which includes a lookup of the tenant that the device belongs to. Thus, the request handler invokes the Tenant HonoClient which will add a task to the *event-loop-thread-1*'s event loop. When the result of the lookup operation is received from the Tenant service (still on *event-loop-thread-1*) the HonoClient completes the result future and the processing of the HTTP request can continue. This involves invocation of `Router.next()` in order to determine the next handler to invoke for processing the HTTP request. However, the Router instance (which has been created on *event-loop-thread-0* when the HTTP server has been started), will now be concurrently accessed from two threads: *event-loop-thread-1* (with the result of the tenant lookup) as well as from *event-loop-thread-0* (for handling the next request coming in from a device).

We now have a situation where two threads try to lock on the same objects (the `Route`s registered in the Router) which seems to be prone to ending in the observed deadlock situation.

I think that we will need to make sure that the result of the operations invoked on the HonoClient instances gets processed on the calling code's Context (and underlying thread). I am currently thinking about ways how to achieve this.

[2018-07-12T08:07:06Z | sophokles73 | comment]
As a corollary to the strategy of fixing this issue, we also need to get the validation of client certificates off of the event loop because the `TenantApiBasedX509TrustManager` uses the `HonoClient` for the Tenant service to look up the tenant that the device belongs to. However, since the `X509TrustManager.checkClientTrusted` method is blocking the current thread, we cannot run both on the same event loop (we would never get the result of the tenant lookup because the result handler is scheduled to the same event loop which is still blocked by the trust manager check).

Assuming that we still want to do validation of client certs based on the dynamic lookup of the trust anchor, we will need to move the validation of the certificate chain up to the application level, i.e. into the `X509AuthHandler`. This actually is less frightening as it at first seems because we need to lookup the tenant there anyway in order to be able to do the credentials lookup (which is always scoped to the tenant).

I might have introduced this bug during splitting the lora app server logic out of loraserver. What happens is: The counter (32 bit) is incremented to 65536 at the side of the node (this value is used for the MIC) and because of this, the `FCnt` which is 16 bit is transmitted as 0, as it contains the 16 LSB. The server is able to detect the 16 bit rollover, but because the MIC validation is happening before the `FCnt` expansion, it is using the wrong `FCnt` to validate the MIC (so it is validated against 0 instead of 65536). I have a fix working locally and will add a testcase to make sure this regression won't be re-introduced again :-) [2016-11-14T19:47:44Z | brocaar | comment] See https://github.com/brocaar/loraserver/commit/2849d0298ce44153876b878183043b5a5f5b9747 for the fix. 1. Start iothub device client (using MQTT, x509 auth);

> At this point there are several "Failure: getaddrinfo failure -3" failures, indicating the name resolution in the system is faulty.

`ifconfig eth0 up`

So at this point the iothub device client is still trying to reconnect, but failing with getaddrinfo setting errno to -3. That is expected since the platform is not providing name resolution to the SDK.

Then, I proceed with these steps to attempt to fix the name resolution:

5. Release the previous address reservation:
`dhclient -r eth0`
6. Renew the address lease:
`dhclient eth0`
> Now verified that name resolution is work again, running `ping www.bing.com`.
7. Verified that iothub device client could now reconnect on its own.

Once the platform started providing name resolution correctly, the IoT hub device client could reconnect.

Note: used a Hyper-V VM running Debian 9.5.0 amd64.

[2017-04-25T00:32:56Z | geekbozu | comment]
So I think this block is not needed, and removing it fixes the problem.

https://github.com/spark/firmware/blob/57fd7cbc3a16ec6cd2e4829eb62a72800fd1a7cd/hal/src/core/i2c_hal.c#L660-L666

The comment claims that with clock stretching enabled it will pull SCL low if DR is empty. However this is only partially true.

The stm will only stretch the clock if it believes it has more data to send. It decides if there is more data to send based on the Master's ACK/NACK of the last transfered byte. If it recieves an ACK it will stretch the clock until the next byte is ready to be shifted out. How-ever if it recieves a nack it will not hold the clock as according to the [I2C specification](http://cache.nxp.com/documents/user_manual/UM10204.pdf) that is how the master signals to the slave that the current transfer is over. 

#### Other
I believe this also applies to the photon/electron as well. According to the reference manual for those devices the same logic as above is applied.

#### Source: 
http://www.st.com/content/ccc/resource/technical/document/reference_manual/59/b9/ba/7f/11/af/43/d5/CD00171190.pdf/files/CD00171190.pdf/jcr:content/translations/en.CD00171190.pdf

[2018-08-27T08:10:07Z | mdicke2s | review:CHANGES_REQUESTED]
Hi @gerrieg 

As I understood the code, the `SocketHandler` is responsible for opening&closing sockets. This happens on every call of `BinRpcClient#sendMessage(int, RpcRequest<byte[]>)`. It gets recreated every time when `config.getSocketMaxAlive()` seconds have passed. Moreover it gets closed immediately as soon as a `BinRpcMessage` was processed by `BinRpcResponseHandler`. 

Having this contribution merged, the `BinRpcResponseHandler` does not close the socket after receiving a callback, but stays listening. Is that related to one of the existing bugs?

`BinRpcResponseHandler` as well as `SocketHandler` will both close the socket after SocketMaxAlive is reached. Assuming that this doesn't necessarily happen at the same time, it is possible that `BinRpcResponseHandler` closes a socket that just has been opened by `SocketHandler` a moment ago. Therefore I wonder if it is malicious to have this close twice in the codebase. What do you think?

[2018-08-28T14:07:42Z | htreu | review_comment]

[2018-08-29T07:00:40Z | gerrieg | comment]
> Having this contribution merged, the BinRpcResponseHandler does not close the socket after receiving a callback, but stays listening. Is that related to one of the existing bugs?

Yes, when java closes a socket, the underlying OS sets the socket to a WAIT state and removes it after some time. If there are many events in a short time, some users report that they are running out of sockets and the communication stops (e.g in Docker). It is also not necessary to always close the socket.

> BinRpcResponseHandler as well as SocketHandler will both close the socket after SocketMaxAlive is reached. Assuming that this doesn't necessarily happen at the same time, it is possible that BinRpcResponseHandler closes a socket that just has been opened by SocketHandler a moment ago

This can't happen. The SocketHandler is only for requests TO the gateway. It is not used for responses FROM the gateway.

And yes of course, i don't need the closeSocket calls if it is also in the finally block. I also changed the logging level.

[2018-08-29T07:32:58Z | mdicke2s | comment]
Thanks for addressing my feedback. I guess growing number sockets is a common source of failure in smarthome systems, so I appreciate to keep the socket open :+1: 

> This can't happen. The SocketHandler is only for requests TO the gateway. It is not used for responses FROM the gateway.

That is correct.... Sorry, I must have mixed two things there. Looking again at the code I see that those sockets are entirely independent:

- `SocketHandler` (which is used in `BinRpcClient#sendMessage(int, RpcRequest<byte[]>)` comes with socket on "gatewayAddress"-IP and "rfPort"
- `BinRpcResponseHandler` comes with socket on "callbackHost"-IP and "binCallbackPort".

Maybe I was mislead by the description of `socketMaxAlive`. According to `HomematicConfig.java` as well as `README.MD`:

> The maximum lifetime of a pooled socket connection **to** the Homematic gateway in seconds

Well, it seems actually like a minor issue, but to avoid confusion, I would suggest to either:

- have two separate `socketMaxAlive` parameters (in/out)
- adjust the description to make clear that it is used for both

[2018-08-29T08:03:00Z | gerrieg | comment]

As discussed, the idea of the getOrCreate..() method and the map is not to cache the command consumer after closed state, but to be able to get the already established and open receiver link, when a device sends command ready events.

[2018-07-09T17:09:52Z | sophokles73 | comment]
@pellmann @sysexcontrol 

> This is especially important for connection based adapters like MQTT but also with e.g. HTTP it could happen, that the device sends an other event with ttd while the receiver link is already opened by an other one and should not be created a second time but reused.

For MQTT I see the benefit of caching the already established link and re-using the command consumer because the consumed commands (from the application) will always be published using the same `MqttEndpoint` instance representing the device. However, in the HTTP adapter, a cached link + consumer will always need to be associated with a new `RoutingContext` (representing the device's current request). We need to make sure that the consumer, which has been originally associated with the link at creation time, is not *overwritten* by a new consumer (for a new request from the same device) before the original consumer has finished its work, i.e. sending back a command to the device. I have not thought this through yet, but I guess it is worth spending one or two thoughts on whether this can actually happen or not.

[2018-07-10T07:47:50Z | sysexcontrol | comment]
@sophokles73 @pellmann 
If we have e.g. two parallel HTTP requests from the same device with a `ttd` set, we would have following scenario IMHO:
- first request comes in and a receiver link is opened
- second request comes in at
  - the same instance: the receiver link is reused, which is associated with the first `RoutingContext`
  - another instance: an additional receiver link is opened, which is associated with a different `RoutingContext` (even in a different JVM)

Next the application receives the downstream message with `ttd` and sends a command upstream:
- if the two requests were opened in the same instance: the command is written to the `RoutingContext` of the first HTTP request
- if the two requests were opened in different instances: the AMQP network decides which of the two links gets the command, and this determines which of the two HTTP requests will receive the command in the response. This assumes we have the routing setup in `balanced` mode.

Additionally we have the scenario that the `ttd` of one of the two requests expires:
- if the two requests were opened in the same instance: the link will be effectively closed, which disables the application to successfully send the command to the second request (since no link is open anymore). This is detectable by the application and can always happen if there would be network problems in delivering the command to the device anyway, so it can be considered as not being an error - the application has to repeat the command later.
- if the two requests were opened in different instances: then the other request will receive the command and puts it to the response.

The described scenario should behave the same with more than two parallel requests, so it should be sufficient to show it for two requests instead of `n` requests.

I hope I did not miss anything - and I will verify the behaviour of the described scenarios (was not done yet).

In general it is a good question IMHO if the scenario of multiple HTTP requests with `ttd` parameters is a realistic scenario - nevertheless it must never malfunction, of course. But the impact that the application may have to repeat a command in special cases (see above) should be acceptable since it might be an unusual use case. Any thoughts on that?

- 3 Generate Script Model.launch
- 4 Generate Rule Model.launch
- 5 Generate Persistence Model.launch

Hi @ertanden 

there is actually the `actiondId` within the DMF AMQP message as `long` in the body of the message. Maybe not the best to just send the `actionId` as long in the body. 
The current message looks like
```
(
   Body:'2' 
   MessageProperties [
              headers=
               {    topic=CANCEL_DOWNLOAD, 
                    content-type=application/json, type=EVENT, 
                    tenant=DEFAULT, 
                    __TypeId__=java.lang.Long, 
                   thingId=dmfSimulated0}, 
                   consumerQueue=simulator_receiver
........
)
```

I guess there is missing the json-document in the body which should probably look like 
```
{
   "actionId" : 1
}
```

I'll keep this issue open as bug for the DMF cancel message body content to serve `application/json` instead of the just the `actionId` as long value because the `content-type: application/json` is actually set in the headers.

Hope this helps,
Cheers,
Michael

[2016-12-19T10:15:31Z | amitjoy | comment]
This is a design decision that we have to consider thinking of its pros and cons in OSGi dynamic environment. You are absolutely right. It is not possible to change the implementation at runtime. It has a history behind it.

`Asset` is a concept that is introduced with `Wires`. `Asset` is a logical representation of device in `Kura` (not restricted to `Wires`). To perform read/write operations on a physical device, users can use `Asset-Driver component model `in `Kura`. We provide the base implementation of `Asset` in `BaseAsset`.

`Asset` is also used as a logical node or `Wire Component` in `Kura Wires` dataflow graph. As `BaseAsset` provides all the necessary implementations to associate `Driver` for reading and writing data from physical devices, `WireAsset` (An implementation of `Asset` and `WireComponent`) leverages the basic implementation of `Asset` (`BaseAsset`).

Now, why did we extend `BaseAsset`?

To leverage the implemented functionalities of `Asset`. So, when an user uses `Wires` with a `WireAsset` configured the the dataflow graph (`Wire Graph`), only one service component is registered - `WireAsset`. And when an user uses `Asset-Driver component model` without `Wires`, only `Asset` service component is registered. 

Why `BaseAsset` is not associated with `WireAsset`?

The lifecycles of `BaseAsset` and `WireAsset` are managed by OSGi configuration service and hence, we didn't choose to create `BaseAsset` manually and inject to `WireAsset`. This could have prevented us to manage the lifecycle of `BaseAsset` in runtime. That's why `WireAsset` does not associate `BaseAsset` but extends.

Yes, you can deploy SiteWhere without using Rook.io.

Assuming that you had a storageClass names `hostpath` on your system, you can install SiteWhere using: 

```console
helm install --name sitewhere \
--set sitewhere-infra-database.mongodb.persistence.storageClass=hostpath \
--set sitewhere-infra-core.kafka.persistence.storageClass=hostpath \
--set sitewhere-infra-core.kafka.zookeeper.persistence.storageClass=hostpath \
sitewhere/sitewhere
```
The installed directory would depend on the `storageClass` you use.

See issue #11. The problem is that the GPIO pins on the board cannot be switched fast enough as required by the Charlieplexing algorithm to work properly. The LoL Shield has 12 pins to drive the LEDs so if you want a refresh rate of 50Hz you'll need to write the pins at 12 x 50 = 600 Hz. The GPIO pins will do about 230 Hz as listed in the Galileo F.A.Q. (https://communities.intel.com/docs/DOC-22543 under Building).

Won't fix as this is a board limitation, besides, the LoL Shield has been discontinued.
